section: Additional Investments – Protecting Canada's Sovereignty and Security
heading: Support for NATO's Ukraine Comprehensive Assistance Package
text: Funding to support the enhancement of Ukraine's security and defence institutions and deter Russian aggression, while also enabling interoperability with NATO. Funding is repurposed from a now-defunct NATO Trust Fund for the Afghan National Army.

chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Comprehensive Expenditure Review
text: Budget 2025 delivers on the Comprehensive Expenditure Review—reducing inefficiency and focusing on core priorities. It will rein in government spending—saving Canada $13 billion annually by 2028-29, for a total with other savings and revenues of $60 billion over five years. Over the last decade, from 2015 to 2024, the federal public service grew by more than 40 per cent—double the rate of economic growth. After direct program expenses began to fall from their COVID-19 peak in 2020-21, the federal public service continued to expand. These increases are unsustainable. This has left federal finances strained, and put the vital services and programs that Canadians rely on at risk. Savings will be achieved by restructuring operations and consolidating internal services and rightsizing programs to realize efficiencies. It will also involve workforce adjustments and attrition to return the size of the public service to a more sustainable level. We will also take action to close tax loopholes and make sure everyone is paying their fair share. To meet the moment, we must reinvent government to be fit for the 21st century. This means recalibrating activities and fiscal room towards our core mandates—spending less on the day-to-day running of government. From a peak of almost 368,000 in 2023-24, the public service population is expected to reach roughly 330,000 by the end of 2028-29—a decline of about 40,000 positions or 10 per cent. This reflects normal attrition through retirements, voluntary departures, and previous savings exercises, as well as further action the government is taking to slow spending and return the public service to a sustainable size. Through the Comprehensive Expenditure Review, and the introduction of new and better tools such as AI, the tech-enabled public service of the future will still deliver the services that Canadians depend on. The Comprehensive Expenditure Review will return government spending to sustainable levels—enabling the government to direct federal spending to enhance productivity and towards capital formation. Each Minister has been tasked with reviewing spending within their portfolio to assess which programs: are meeting their objectives are core to the federal mandate, and complement—rather than duplicate—services delivered by other federal departments or levels of government. This review is not an across-the-board reduction exercise. It is a measured and strategic approach to improve public service productivity. To achieve this objective, federal departments and agencies undertook a thorough review of their organizations, identifying programs and activities that were underperforming, duplicative or that had strayed away from the core federal mandate. Departments were directed to develop proposals using Gender-Based Analysis Plus to understand how Canadians, including vulnerable groups, would be affected. Statutory transfers payments to provinces, territories and individuals were outside the scope of the review. The Department of Finance and Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat worked with departments to ensure their proposals were sustainable and did not create program integrity pressures or impact the health, safety and the national security of Canadians. Furthermore, the government ensured the proposals did not materially impact core science, research and Indigenous programming. Evaluation of the proposals was done thoroughly, with strong governance. The Cabinet Committee on Government Transformation / Government Efficiency reviewed all proposals to ensure appropriate oversight and to apply a consistent, whole-of-government approach. Following Cabinet's review, the Minister of Finance and Prime Minister made final decisions for inclusion in Budget 2025. With this review, the government is making responsible choices to modernise government, right-size programs, improve efficiencies, and deliver better results and services for Canadians. By spending less, we can make the generational investments that grow our economy and protect the essential programs that keep your costs down. The Comprehensive Expenditure Review will achieve savings of $9 billion in 2026-27, $10 billion in 2027-28 and $13 billion in 2028-29. Combined with other savings and revenues in Budget 2025, this will total $60 billion over five years, starting in 2025-26. Detailed allocations of savings by portfolio are available in Annex 3. Planned savings fall under three themes generally: Modernising Government Operations, Streamlining Program Delivery, and Recalibrating Government Programs. Modernising Government Operations: The federal government needs to change how it operates and how things are being done to address the challenges we are facing as a country. This theme includes increasing the efficiency of back-office and administrative functions, leveraging new technology, and limiting spending on discretionary travel and training, and the use of external consultants ($25.2 billion over four years). Streamlining Program Delivery: Identifying the right federal program to help you, your family or your business can be complicated and confusing. To make programs more accessible for Canadians and improve administrative efficiency, several federal organizations will streamline their program delivery to improve services and reduce duplication ($1.5 billion over four years). Recalibrating Government Programs: To better align federal funding with the needs of Canadians and priorities of today and tomorrow, the government has identified opportunities to refocus several programs. This will help prioritize programs that will deliver the greatest impact ($17.5 billion over four years). Consistent with a focus on improving productivity and efficiency, more than half of the total savings originate from actions to modernize government operations. This will contribute to reducing projected growth in the government's day-to-day operating spending, while maintaining programs and major transfers to Canadians. The government recalibrated programs through this exercise in order to deliver on the new generational investments in infrastructure, housing, and sectoral support provided in Budget 2025. While this review has involved tough choices, these adjustments make sense to ensure responsible use of public funds while delivering the support Canadians expect from their government. Through the review, the focus has been on linking both spending and savings to key outcomes, a number of which are presented below. By 2028-29, reductions from the Comprehensive Expenditure Review will represent 4.9 per cent of projected direct program expenses. These reductions are consistent with exercises taken in previous years to ensure that the federal government's finances are sustainable. Chart 5.2 illustrates the reductions from previous review exercises at maturity as a share of projected direct program expenses. Savings across departments and programs vary, reflecting the need to protect the important mandates that some organizations have in delivering frontline services, social programs, and priorities such as defence and security. Recognizing recent investments and the importance of securing Canada's sovereignty, security and border, the Department of National Defence, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Canada Border Services Agency's annual savings target was set at two per cent of the review base. Given their essential role in keeping our country safe, this approach is also being taken with the Canadian Security Intelligence Service and the Communications Security Establishment. A resilient Canadian economy needs to advance research and attract and retain the top research talent to supercharge our growth. Recognizing this priority, the targets of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research are also being set at two per cent, to protect the councils' important contributions in improving our global competitiveness and contributing to the economy of the future. The Department for Women and Gender Equality (WAGE) empowers women and 2SLGBTQI+ people through programs to eliminate discrimination and advance the rights of women and 2SLGBTQI+ communities. To support WAGE in continuing this critical work, its annual savings target is being set at two per cent of its review base. The government remains committed to reconciliation. Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada and Indigenous Services Canada deliver important programs that are legally or constitutionally required, including child and family services, primary health care, and essential community infrastructure. The government will review how these organizations can deliver these programs more efficiently, with a two per cent savings target. Actions taken through the Comprehensive Expenditure Review to reduce day-to-day operating spending complement other fiscal actions in Budget 2025, including proposing a reverse charge mechanism to help combat carousel fraud schemes and proposed legislative amendments to reform and modernize transfer pricing rules, to protect the integrity of Canada's tax system and ensure the government collects revenues that it should.

chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Workforce Renewal
text: The savings identified through CER will contribute to returning the size of the public service to a more sustainable level, with an estimated reduction of 16,000 full-time equivalents, or roughly 4.5 per cent of the workforce as of March 2025. Of these reductions, some 650 will be executive positions, representing about 7 per cent of the executive population. These reductions will continue the trend towards a more sustainable public service size of roughly 330,000 by 2028-29, a decline of about 40,000 or 10 per cent from the 2023-24 peak—where attrition has, and will continue to be, a driver. The government understands that transitions can be difficult and is committed to minimising hardship for federal employees, while also protecting diversity in the public service workforce and ensuring a strong, younger generation of public servants. This is a transformational time for the public service to revisit how we work, how we can improve services to Canadians and how we can build for the future. A leaner public service is a more empowered and productive public service. To manage these reductions to the greatest extent possible through attrition and voluntary departures, Budget 2025 proposes to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Income Tax Regulations to offer a voluntary Early Retirement Incentive (ERI) program through the Public Service Pension Plan. Public servants at age 50 or above for Group 1 and age 55 or above for Group 2 who have at least ten years of employment, with at least two years of pensionable service in the Plan may apply to participate under parameters set by Treasury Board. These parameters will be designed to maintain essential services and business continuity. Eligible employees will be able to retire with an immediate pension based on years of service with no penalty for early retirement. Implementation would proceed by January 15, 2026, or when legislation receives Royal Assent, and the government intends to conclude the ERI process within one year. This program, which will be sourced from the Public Service Pension Fund, is estimated to have a net fiscal impact of $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2025-26, while providing ongoing savings of $82.0 million annually. To support the increased workflow at the Government of Canada Pension Centre from administering this time-limited program, Budget 2025 proposes to provide Public Services and Procurement Canada with $15.0 million over two years, starting in 2025-26. As the size of the public service adjusts, so too, must the leadership. The government will reduce the executive cadre in the public service by 1,000 positions overall over the next two years, inclusive of positions reduced through CER and early retirements. The government will also reduce expenses on management and other consulting services by 20 per cent in three years' time – in order to reduce wasteful spending and empower the public service to take on more responsibility and accountability. These actions will ensure that the public service continues to provide effective services while being representative of the Canadians that it serves and fostering the next generation of public servants. In the coming weeks, participating organizations will be communicating these measures to their employees and collective bargaining agents. The federal government will continue to identify more efficiencies and potential savings, which will be communicated in the 2026-27 Main Estimates and Departmental Plans.

chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Optimizing Productivity in Government
text: To ensure high quality service delivery for Canadians, the government must continually strive to optimize its productivity and transform how it operates. The government will make sure public servants are equipped with the tools, technology and training to do their jobs. We will bring focus to our priorities. We will clarify accountabilities. We will simplify processes and reduce duplication. This is about doing things faster, simpler and better. At the same time, as emerging technologies like AI continue to advance, the government intends to be at the forefront in their adoption and build and rely on the skills we have in the public service. Budget 2025 announces that going forward, the government will: Improve expenditure management by adopting a regular, predictable review schedule to ensure continuous optimization of resources. Future reviews will focus on specific horizontal themes, such as consolidating the administration of programs, fostering AI implementation and scale-up in the public service, and reviewing business subsidies and skills programming. To demonstrate the government's commitment to restraining the growth in day-to-day operating spending, it is targeting additional savings of $7.75 billion over three years, starting in 2027-28, and $3.25 billion ongoing. Results will be reported on in Budget 2026.

id: 2025|chap5-en.html|Adopting AI to Enhance Productivity and Improve Services
chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Adopting AI to Enhance Productivity and Improve Services
text: Budget 2025 announces that the government intends to stand up an Office of Digital Transformation which will proactively identify, implement, and scale technology solutions across the federal government—a generational opportunity for domestic innovators. The Office will identify and eliminate redundant and counterproductive procurement rules as well as leverage expertise from internal sources and the private sector to hasten AI adoption. Budget 2025 also announces that Shared Services Canada, in partnership with the Department of National Defence and the Communications Security Establishment, will develop a made-in-Canada AI tool that can be deployed across the federal government. Shared Services Canada will partner with leading Canadian AI companies to develop this internal tool. By supporting innovative research to strengthen public services, this work will protect our digital sovereignty, keep government data and information safe in Canada, and create opportunities for the Canadian technology sector. Through the Comprehensive Expenditure Review, departments have identified ways to use technology to achieve savings by streamlining workflows, reducing manual effort and optimising service delivery. Shared Services Canada will apply AI and automation across internal operations, and automate common IT support requests, reducing call volumes and costs while improving the user experience. The Department of Justice will integrate AI, advanced analytics and automation tools to streamline routine tasks, enhance decision-making and free employees to focus on higher-value strategic work. Transport Canada will use AI and automation to optimise back-office activities and reduce costs of dedicated resources assigned to repetitive tasks, and realign service delivery models with a greater focus on self-service and technology-enabled solutions. Public Services and Procurement Canada will implement digital delivery of procurement-related documents to better manage project delivery.

chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Equitable Public Sector Retirement Benefits
text: In 2019, enhancements to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and the Quebec Pension Plan (QPP) led federal employees and the government to contribute more than needed to maintain existing pension benefits. Budget 2025 announces the government's intention to initiate consultations with key stakeholders to account for CPP and QPP enhancements and ensure that federal employees continue to receive the same pension benefits, without overcontributing. This will save federal employees up to $1,100 in annual pension contributions, while maintaining their pension benefit levels. At the same time, this will achieve fiscal savings of $1.1 billion over four years, starting in 2026-27, and $384 million ongoing from lower pension expenses for the government. In 2014, the government increased the number of years of service required to be eligible for the Public Service Health Care Plan in retirement from two to six, to ensure that the costs of the Public Service Health Care Plan remained sustainable and affordable in the future. To ensure benefits remain available to public servants in retirement, while being reasonable for taxpayers: Budget 2025 announces that the government will consult stakeholders on making similar modifications to the Pensioners' Dental Services Plan so that, going forward, the years of service required to be eligible to participate in the Plan in retirement would increase from two to six years. This will not impact current members. With these changes implemented before the end of the 2025-26 fiscal year, net savings of $101.8 million over five years, starting in 2025-26, and $13.1 million per year ongoing are expected.

chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Collective Bargaining in Good Faith
text: 2025 marks the beginning of a new round of collective bargaining between federal public service bargaining agents and the government. The government believes that the best deals are reached by the parties at the bargaining table. In working to renew collective agreements, the government will negotiate fair and reasonable agreements that balance the interests of both employees and taxpayers. At the same time, the government will respect workers' fundamental rights to organize, collectively bargain, and commence legal labour actions. Budget 2025 reaffirms these rights by proposing to introduce amendments to the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act to ensure the government can attract and retain the necessary talent for a high-performing public service to meet the needs of Canadians, while respecting Canada's fiscal circumstances relative to its stated budgetary policies and objectives. Public sector compensation must align with Canadian labour market trends and the government's fiscal position, freeing resources to be invested towards growing Canada's economy.

id: 2025|chap5-en.html|Improving the Integrity of Student Financial Assistance
chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Improving the Integrity of Student Financial Assistance
text: The Canada Student Financial Assistance Program plays an important role in facilitating access to post-secondary education—providing opportunities for Canadians to learn new skills and earn new qualifications. Ensuring that it is used as intended is essential to control costs and to provide a fair chance to students who rely on this support. Budget 2025 announces the government's intention to propose legislative and regulatory amendments to address integrity issues related to private educational institutions by generally limiting access to the Canada Student Grant for Full-time Students to students attending public educational institutions and not-for-profit private institutions within Canada. Internationally, Canada Student Loans and Grants generally would only be provided to those who attend public institutions. This measure is expected to result in savings of approximately $1.0 billion over four years, starting in 2026-27, and $280.1 million ongoing. Addressing integrity issues in the Canada Student Financial Assistance Program limits the financial risks to the Crown and ensures that post-secondary students have access to the best educational outcomes.

chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Faster Services for Veterans
text: Canada owes a debt of gratitude to the women and men who answered the call to serve. Canada's Veterans should never have to wait unnecessarily for the services they have earned—they deserve timely, compassionate support. While recent temporary funding injections have increased processing capacity, which has enabled reductions to wait times and the backlog, Veterans Affairs Canada continues to face pressure from rising caseloads. To that end: Budget 2025 proposes to provide $184.9 million over four years, starting in 2026-27, and $40.1 million ongoing for Veterans Affairs Canada to stabilise their processing capacity for disability benefits applications and to modernise operational processes and IT infrastructure for their disability benefits program.

id: 2025|chap5-en.html|Maintaining the Effectiveness of Fines and Penalties
chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Maintaining the Effectiveness of Fines and Penalties
text: The government levies administrative monetary penalties and fines for violations of certain legislation or regulations. These levies are meant to ensure everyone follows the rules, whether employment standards, environmental regulations, or air passenger rights. In the Strong Borders Act and the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act , the government proposed stronger administrative monetary penalties to strengthen compliance under Canada's Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Terrorist Finance Regime. However, some other fines and penalties have not been reassessed in many years. To ensure that these remain effective: Budget 2025 announces the government's intention to launch a review of fines and penalties to ensure the charges are sufficient and that non-compliance is not just treated as the cost of doing business. Results of the review will be available in Budget 2026.

chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Cutting Regulatory and Operational Red Tape
text: A range of government legislation imposes red tape and regulatory hurdles, while reducing certainty for businesses and Canadians, and hinders broader government efficiency and effectiveness. A less visible form of red tape is legislated requirements that reduce government efficiency and operational effectiveness. These requirements, such as duplicative reporting or cumbersome approvals processes, consume a significant amount of public servants' time, diverting them from tasks that provide greater value to Canadians. In the spirit of the 60-day regulatory review, the government further intends to introduce a variety of targeted amendments to legislation in order to increase government efficiency and operational effectiveness. This includes amendments that would streamline low-risk internal processes, modernise outdated requirements, eliminate unnecessary and burdensome reporting requirements, remove unnecessary barriers to agile regulation-making, align legislative and regulatory authorities across government and provide for the delegation of certain matters where appropriate. Results of this review will be available in Budget 2026.

id: 2025|chap5-en.html|Attracting Private Sector Expertise to the Public Service
chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Attracting Private Sector Expertise to the Public Service
text: There is a need to bring in talent and perspectives from outside the government into the public service at speed and scale. To this end, the government is announcing that the Interchange Canada program will be rebranded as the Build Canada Exchange , with an ambitious, immediate-term goal of integrating 50 external leaders in technology, finance, science, and other sectors into the public service.

id: 2025|chap5-en.html|Protecting the Integrity of the Tax System
chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Protecting the Integrity of the Tax System
text: Budget 2025 proposes new measures to protect the integrity of Canada's tax system, promote a level playing field for taxpayers, and address abusive tax practices. These tax integrity measures are expected to collectively increase federal revenues by hundreds of millions of dollars. To improve tax fairness, Budget 2025 proposes to amend the Income Tax Act to limit the deferral of refundable tax on investment income through the use of tiered corporate structures with staggered year ends, for taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day. To ensure that Canadian multinational insurers do not avoid tax on their Canadian insurance business by operating through a foreign subsidiary, Budget 2025 proposes to amend the Income Tax Act to clarify that income derived from assets held by a foreign affiliate of a Canadian insurance company that support Canadian insurance risks is taxable in Canada. To protect the integrity of Canada's tax base, Budget 2025 announces the government's intention to propose legislative amendments to reform and modernise the transfer pricing rules, which are used to determine profit among the various entities of a multinational enterprise group. To protect Canada's revenue base, Budget 2025 proposes a new reverse charge mechanism to help combat carousel fraud schemes under the Goods and Services Tax/Harmonized Sales Tax, beginning with the telecommunications sector.

id: 2025|chap5-en.html|Improving the Efficiency of the Tax System
chapter: Creating a more efficient and effective government
heading: Improving the Efficiency of the Tax System
text: Budget 2025 proposes to eliminate or modify tax measures that have proven to be inefficient, costly to administer, and challenging for Canadian industries at a time of ongoing global economic uncertainty. To provide relief to the aviation and boating industries and increase the overall efficiency of the luxury tax framework, Budget 2025 announces the government's intention to end the luxury tax on aircraft and vessels as of the day after Budget Day. To simplify Canada's tax system and reduce compliance costs for taxpayers and administrative costs for government, and given other efforts such as the federal foreign buyer ban and municipal and provincial vacant home taxes, Budget 2025 announces the government's intention to eliminate the Underused Housing Tax as of the 2025 calendar year.

id: 2026|chap1-en.html|Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction
section: Making Canada the best place to invest
heading: Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction
text: In September 2026, we announced the Productivity Mega Deduction. Building on the Productivity Super Deduction introduced last year, the Productivity Mega Deduction allows businesses to immediately write off the full cost of a broader range of capital assets, representing more than 65% of investment, on a permanent basis. This gives businesses the certainty they need to make major investment decisions, offering greater cost efficiency, competitiveness, and simplicity. Private investment in new machinery, technology, and other assets is one of the best ways to increase productivity, create jobs, and strengthen long-term growth. With the Productivity Mega Deduction , Canada's marginal effective tax rate (METR) on new business investment will fall from 13% to 6.4%—the lowest in the G7 and less than half the rate in the United States. That makes Canada more tax competitive than the U.S. across all major sectors of the economy. The Productivity Mega Deduction also gives Canada the lowest tax rate on new business investment of any major economy in the world. With an estimated fiscal cost of $36 billion over five years, beginning in 2026-27, it will help create the conditions for an extended period of higher investment: Canada's Investment Supercycle. For businesses, lower effective marginal tax rates increase the after-tax rate of return on new investment, strengthening the incentive to invest in the machinery, equipment, and technologies needed to expand production. Together with the broader package of accelerated depreciation measures introduced since Budget 2025, the Productivity Mega Deduction will support higher investment and capital accumulation across sectors, expanding the economy's productive capacity over time. Ranges Refrigerators Preparation tables Grills Food processors Mixers Dishwashing equipment Dining-room furniture Point-of-sale hardware Overhead bridge cranes Hoists Blow-in insulation machines Laser-cutting equipment Computer-guided routing machines Welding equipment Assembly-line conveyors Quality-control scanners Jackhammers Excavators Bulldozers Mobile cranes Concrete mixers Graders Loaders Backhoes Dump trucks Tractors Combine harvesters Farm trailers Plows Seeders Crop sprayers Balers Forage harvesters Frame, log, or corrugated metal barns used for farming Greenhouses Silos Sorting machines Industrial washers Peelers Industrial grinders Blanchers Homogenisers Pasteurisers Bottling equipment Conveyors Filling/sealing/ labelling machines Fishing vessels Nets Hooks Ice makers Winches Fish-finders On-board refrigeration equipment Log, frame, or corrugated metal buildings used for fishing Hotel beds and other furniture Refrigerators Laundry machines Fitness equipment TVs Coach buses Sightseeing vessels Chairlifts/gondolas Snow-making and grooming equipment Amusement park rides Medical imaging equipment (X-rays, ultrasound) ECG monitors Pulmonary-function monitors Specialised examination chairs Sterilisation equipment Laboratory analysers Office furniture Medical and dental tools Aircraft Baggage loaders De-icing equipment Vessels Heavy freight trucks Larger buses Railway track Locomotives and railway cars Cameras and video-recording equipment Lighting equipment Sound-recording equipment Mixing consoles Projection equipment Stage rigging Editing workstations Studio furniture This list of assets is illustrative. Once legislation is tabled, the Canada Revenue Agency will be responsible for determining whether specific assets qualify for the Productivity Mega Deduction based on the facts of each particular case. The limited exclusions from the Productivity Mega Deduction are generally either very long-lived assets, assets that have a significant personal use component, or assets subject to regulated rates. These exclusions generally align with exclusions under 100% bonus depreciation provided in the U.S. The Canadian approach to immediate expensing is competitive for investors compared with the United States. The Productivity Mega Deduction excludes a limited range of assets, generally consisting of certain long-lived buildings and intangibles, certain passenger vehicles, regulated natural gas distribution pipelines, and property subject to specialised resource-depletion rules. U.S. 100% bonus depreciation generally excludes tangible property depreciated over more than 20 years and certain other property. Longer-lived buildings, most intangible property, and property used in specified rate-regulated utility businesses generally do not qualify. Passenger vehicles are either excluded or the amount of bonus depreciation is subject to a dollar limit.

id: 2026|chap1-en.html|Rewarding innovation by helping Canadian ideas and talent succeed
section: Making Canada the best place to invest
heading: Rewarding innovation by helping Canadian ideas and talent succeed
text: New ideas, technologies, and businesses create jobs, raise incomes, and keep Canada's economy globally competitive. Canada is home to many talented entrepreneurs, skilled researchers, and innovators. But turning a good idea into a successful business requires access to capital, talented workers, and opportunities to grow. Budget 2026 will help Canadian businesses and talent succeed. Its measures will improve access to growth capital, attract world-class talent to our growing sectors, and strengthen support for research and commercialisation opportunities while protecting intellectual property. By boosting and rewarding Canadian innovation, we are helping more of our businesses start, scale, and compete worldwide.

section: Making Canada the best place to invest
heading: Backing Canada's next generation of entrepreneurs
text: Canada shares a border with one of the world's largest economic powers. To compete, we must be ambitious and ensure Canadian entrepreneurs have the opportunities, access to capital, and confidence they need to build and grow here at home. Canadian high-growth startups drive innovation across the economy. Yet too often, their lack of access to growth capital holds them back. Talent and ideas leave Canada and take root elsewhere. To counter this, Canada must aggressively compete to attract and retain those that will create the next generation of Canadian businesses. That demands strong, pro-entrepreneurial action. That's why Budget 2026 takes bold steps to strengthen Canada's innovation ecosystem by increasing the incentives for risk-taking, enabling successful investors and founders to reinvest in new Canadian companies while mobilising new domestic capital to support Canadian businesses. This includes: Introducing the Canada Growth Incentive to help high-potential businesses attract investment and grow in Canada, consisting of two measures: introducing a new tax exemption for Canadian builders on up to $15 million in capital gains earned from successful investments in eligible Canadian companies and enhancing the small business rollover to allow increased deferral of taxes on capital gains when proceeds are reinvested in another Canadian small business. By allowing builders to keep more of the benefits when a business succeeds, these measures will help level the playing field with the United States, encourage more capital to flow to Canadian businesses, and enable successful entrepreneurs to reinvest their proceeds into Canada. This incentive would provide $715 million in tax relief over four years, starting in 2027-28. Together, these measures would mean that a founder has a stronger incentive to build a valuable company in Canada, an early-stage employee sees more upside in accepting equity as part of their compensation, and an investor gets a better potential after-tax return for backing a promising Canadian company. For a founder with a $15 million capital gain, that difference is substantial: they would retain nearly 96% of the value when they exit, compared with 71% before Budget 2026. The Canada Growth Incentive will be one of the most significant incentives to attract and retain builders here in Canada. By creating the path for entrepreneurs, investors, and employees to reinvest in Canada, we are firmly backing our builders to drive innovation, growth, and jobs, ensuring that Canada does not face a "brain drain." Combined with the Productivity Mega Deduction , this represents a level shift in the attractiveness of firms, large and small, to invest—and reinvest—in Canada, and deliver lasting prosperity for all Canadians.

section: Making Canada the best place to invest
heading: Helping Canadian innovators scale at home
text: Canada's economic security depends on innovative Canadian founders who start companies, commercialise new ideas, and scale up their businesses while remaining anchored to Canada. That is how we create good jobs at home and reap the greatest benefits from our world-class workforce and ingenuity. Canada's Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy , first announced in Budget 2025, addresses persistent financing gaps facing Canada's most promising firms. Through up to $750 million in investments, offered on a cash basis, the Strategy will mobilise domestic private capital and help Canadian companies grow and scale right here in Canada. Delivered by the Business Development Bank of Canada, the Strategy includes: Pre-seed and Seed Investment Stream: $75 million to support investment in innovative early-stage companies. Later and Growth Stage Investment Stream: $675 million to increase the availability of domestic growth capital for Canadian companies as they expand and scale. Together, these streams will help more promising Canadian companies access the capital they need to grow and scale here at home.

section: Making Canada the best place to invest
heading: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text: Canada's research and innovation agenda is entering a pivotal phase. Major projects are moving forward at speed and scale, and significant investments are being made in research, innovation, and emerging technologies. This is a competitive advantage for Canada. We have long been a global leader in these fields, and we can fuel our long-term economic growth and competitiveness by strongly supporting science and innovation. At a time when other countries are pulling back from research, Canada is doubling down. We are putting policies in place that attract leading researchers, innovators, and entrepreneurs from around the world, giving them the opportunity to contribute here. Canadian businesses need a tax system that supports businesses of all sizes, from research and development through to commercialisation. Last year, we enhanced and simplified the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program by expanding access to the enhanced credit, restoring support for capital expenditures, and increasing the annual eligible expenditure limit on which the enhanced credit can be earned to $6 million to help businesses innovate and grow. To build on this momentum: Budget 2026 proposes to further expand the SR&ED tax incentive program to include certain commercialisation expenses. Eligible expenditures would be expanded to include certain costs associated with bringing a new product or process to market, including obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications, and securing and maintaining intellectual property protection. This measure would apply to expenditures incurred in taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day. This measure is expected to provide support of $930 million over five years, with $235 million ongoing. In addition, the Canada Revenue Agency will work to provide sector-specific guidance to clarify SR&ED eligibility as it pertains to commercialisation expenses. The inclusion of certain commercialisation expenses under the SR&ED program will provide an additional level of support for builders and businesses performing cutting-edge research and development, translating their intellectual and technological capital into commercial-ready ventures. To fully realise the economic benefits of their new ideas, Canadian businesses must also be able to translate their innovations into commercial success and retain the value they create. This requires a competitive, transparent, and coordinated approach to intellectual property: one that helps Canadian businesses and entrepreneurs retain and capitalise on their ideas right here at home. To support this, Budget 2025 announced the government's intention to undertake a performance review to strengthen Canada's intellectual property ecosystem and support the growth of intellectual-property-intensive firms. Budget 2026 announces several initial measures to deliver on that commitment, including: Modernising policies at Canada's three federal granting councils—the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research—to improve commercialisation rates for publicly funded research. Initiating consultations with experts on how to strengthen technology transfer capacity at post-secondary institutions and help bring more Canadian research to market. Leveraging the expertise, capabilities, and assets of the National Research Council of Canada to identify ways to expand the impact of its intellectual property and support Canadian innovation and economic growth. Amending the Patent Act to require changes in patent ownership to be registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office, giving businesses and investors clearer information about who owns Canadian patents and helping reduce due diligence costs and investment risk. Developing new regulations under the Patent Act to establish minimum requirements for written patent demand letters. This will help protect Canadian businesses from abusive practices, including vague or misleading patent infringement claims intended to extract nuisance payments. Further measures will be announced in spring 2027. Targeted support can also help innovative businesses take on larger, riskier projects, as well as commercialise and scale new technologies. The Strategic Response Fund , initially launched in 2017 as the Strategic Innovation Fund, helps Canadian industries innovate, adapt, and compete by supporting large-scale projects that strengthen Canada's economy. To help bridge market gaps and catalyse investment in promising new innovations across the economy, including in areas like AI, agri-food, bio-manufacturing, and clean technologies: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $1 billion over six years, starting in 2028-29, to the Strategic Response Fund to support large-scale research and development and innovation projects that can strengthen Canada's long-term competitiveness and growth.

id: 2026|chap1-en.html|Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
section: Making Canada the best place to invest
heading: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
text: Canada hosted its first-ever Canada Investment Summit in September 2026, welcoming investors to Toronto and showcasing Canada as the destination of choice for global capital. The Summit brought together investors from nearly 30 countries responsible for managing more than $100 trillion in assets, along with federal ministers, senior officials, provincial representatives, and Indigenous leaders. More than 165 investment opportunities in priority sectors—including energy and critical minerals, artificial intelligence, defence, and infrastructure—were profiled. Investors immediately recognised Canada's strengths and responded to our ambitions; by the end of the Summit, nearly $500 billion in new investment commitments to Canada had been made. As a result of the government's economic plan: Canada's top banks committed nearly $325 billion in new financing for Canadian businesses and infrastructure. Canada's leading pension funds, insurers, and institutional investors committed nearly $100 billion in new capital to Canadian assets. Investment funds committed to mobilise more than $14 billion in capital to grow Canadian companies, infrastructure, and strategic sectors. On the margins of the Summit, Bell Canada, in partnership with the Government of Saskatchewan, announced a historic expansion of the Bell AI Fabric to build a 1.2-gigawatt Canadian AI infrastructure hub in Saskatchewan. This $52.5 billion capital investment is the largest in the province's history and is expected to create more than 4,500 jobs across construction, operations, management, and related services. For Canadians, these investments mean tens of thousands of new jobs for skilled workers in every region of the country. They mean modern, robust infrastructure being built in Canada again—from stronger electricity grids powering our cities to the railways and roads that connect our country. They will fund our aerospace and defence industries of tomorrow while getting shovels in the ground on new mines and data centres today. The Canada Investment Summit advanced our most important mission: building a stronger, more independent, more resilient Canadian economy for all. We remain focused on our goal of catalysing up to $1 trillion in total investment over five years, including $500 billion in new private sector investment. Reaching that goal means keeping Canada top of mind for the world's biggest investors—and making sure that interest translates into investments that help Canadian projects, businesses, and workers. Invest in Canada , the federal agency that works to attract global investment to Canada, will have an expanded role in that effort. To help Invest in Canada deliver on this ambition: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $181.4 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, $50.4 million in future years, and $40.4 million ongoing to expand Invest in Canada to add specialised financial sector expertise and establish its presence in key global markets to bring in capital from major investors and multinational corporations. Invest in Canada will also deliver Canada's future Investment Summits.

id: 2026|chap1-en.html|Mobilising private investment to modernise Canada's airports
section: Making Canada the best place to invest
heading: Mobilising private investment to modernise Canada's airports
text: Canada's airports connect Canadians and support tourism, trade, and economic growth. Airport authorities have built and maintained a safe and reliable airport system for more than three decades. In the years to come, meeting growing demand for air travel, ensuring affordability, and improving the passenger experience will require additional investment and expertise. To prepare Canada's air transportation system for the future, we are seeking private investment through long-term operating concessions for our four largest airports. Under this model, used successfully in other countries, experienced investors, like Canada's pension funds, would operate airports for 40 to 50 years while Canada retains ownership of airport lands and assets. Operators would be subject to strong oversight to protect travellers and the interests of Canadians. The airport fees included in the price of an airline ticket would be subject to clear rules to protect travellers from unreasonable increases. New investment and expertise will improve airport services and infrastructure—making travel more efficient and expanding travel and tourism options. Canadians will share directly in the success of concessions through equity stakes for the Canada Strong Fund and local Indigenous communities. To launch the first airport operating concession, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $37.6 million over three years, starting in 2026-27, to ensure a strong return for Canadians by completing due diligence, developing the concession framework, obtaining specialised commercial and legal advice, and completing a competitive process to select the operator by early 2029. Budget 2026 also proposes to introduce legislation necessary to implement and establish the operating concessions. The transition to the new model is part of the government's broader plan to build a more affordable, connected, and competitive air sector. Fiscal proceeds from the new model will be reinvested to benefit Canadians. They will support improvements across the air transportation system (e.g., regional airports, air connections between communities, and local transportation infrastructure) while helping build the infrastructure Canada needs. This could include helping to finance a sovereign broadband backbone that connects Canadians from coast to coast, with more direct and secure links to Europe and Asia. Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to pursue additional measures—supported by concession proceeds—to improve the experience for travellers. These will prioritise regional connectivity, ensure air travel is affordable, and strengthen the governance and oversight of Canada's airports. Detailed measures will be developed and released over time. They will: Improve access to air travel in regional, remote, and northern communities by supporting new air routes and investing in infrastructure at smaller regional airports. Adjust the ground rent formula to support growth at airports that will continue to operate under the existing model. Introduce legislation to improve transparency around airport fees, strengthen performance reporting and governance, and support economic development and accessibility. Expand eligibility for the Airports Capital Assistance Program to include smaller airports in the National Airports System. Budget 2026 also proposes to provide $4.3 million over four years, starting in 2026-27, to Transport Canada to develop a Traveller Biometrics Strategy . The Strategy will make air travel faster and simpler, including through the potential use of digital credentials that can help travellers move through airports and other points of entry more efficiently. It will bring together airports, airlines, security screening, and border services, while protecting privacy, personal information, accessibility, cybersecurity, and individual choice. A Special Advisor on Traveller Biometrics will be appointed to lead this work and coordinate responsible and secure implementation across industry and government.

section: Building a cleaner, more competitive economy
heading: Powering Canada Strong
text: Canada has the potential to be an energy superpower. We have abundant reserves; hydroelectric, wind, and nuclear capability; and a grid that is already among the cleanest and cheapest in the G7. Building upon this potential is how we secure our sovereignty, increase our exports, and become more self-reliant: it is, as it was for Québec when the term was first coined, an integral piece to being masters of our destiny . Electricity is key to Canada's energy security, sovereignty, and affordability; we know that the nations that master electricity will own the 21st century. Canada starts with advantages: we already have a nearly 80% clean grid and some of the lowest electricity costs among peer nations. But as our economy grows and our industries become more energy-intensive, electricity demand in Canada is expected to double by 2050. This is an enormous opportunity for Canada to build a sustainable, affordable future—but we have to start now. Increasing electrification will boost our energy sovereignty, give Canadian industries a competitive advantage, and lower energy costs for 7 in 10 Canadian families, playing a key part in the government's affordability efforts. A household's "energy wallet" can be thought of as combined payments for gasoline, natural gas, and electricity. Electrification means more and better choice. In the future, the "electricity" slice of the pie will get much bigger, but for most, the entire pie will get smaller since households will be relying on more efficient forms of energy. Budget 2026 is investing over $50 billion in bold and ambitious measures to expand Canada's electricity system, support investment in clean technologies, attract private capital, and provide greater certainty for businesses. These actions will create jobs, strengthen energy security, and ensure Canada remains competitive as the global economy evolves. Announced in May 2026, Canada's National Electricity Strategy outlined how Canada can work with provinces, territories, Indigenous Peoples, utilities, unions, and other partners to double the capacity of our grid by 2050. The Strategy is guided by four pillars and eight key actions: Mastering electricity also means finding the ways that greater electrification can interact and support priorities in other sectors. Canada's Automotive Strategy is helping Canadians choose electric and enhancing Canada's EV charging network, which makes it easier and more convenient for Canadians to drive their electric vehicles more. At the same time, we are helping retrofit one million homes with modern, energy-efficient technologies (including electric heat pumps), reducing energy use, lowering emissions, and helping Canadians save money on their energy bills. The message to the world is clear: if you need clean, affordable power, Canada is your answer. heat pumps installed (2020-26) EV chargers installed (2019-26) EVs on the road heat pumps to be installed (2026-34) EV chargers to be installed (2026-29) heat pumps to be installed by 2033-34 EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29 Budget 2026 builds on this momentum with measures to unlock investment, build capacity for more generation and transmission, and improve the reliability of electricity systems across the country, so that we can power Canada Strong. The Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits help catalyse and unlock investment across the economy, from renewable energy systems to electricity transmission. To provide the certainty needed for longer-term projects, Budget 2026 proposes to extend the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits to the end of 2040. For the Clean Technology investment tax credit, the phase-out to 15% would occur in 2040 rather than 2034. To encourage more investment in electricity transmission, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligibility for the Clean Electricity investment tax credit to the highest-voltage intra-provincial electricity transmission lines in each province, for property acquired and available for use on or after Budget Day. Combined, these measures are expected to cost $2.4 billion from 2027-28 to 2030-31 and $36.1 billion from 2031-32 to 2041-42. As global supply chains evolve and economic partnerships are reshaped, Canada must ensure that Canadian workers and industries fully benefit from new investment opportunities. The Government is committed to this objective. To meet that commitment, the Government will conduct targeted consultations with stakeholders over the next 60 days to determine the scope and parameters of a domestic content bonus of up to 10 percentage points under the Clean Technology investment tax credit and up to 5 percentage points under the Clean Electricity investment tax credit . This will support the use of Canadian industrial products in the projects needed to double Canada's production and transmission of electricity. In addition, Budget 2026 proposes further investments to expand, strengthen, and better connect Canada's electricity systems. To deliver more reliable power as electricity demand grows, Budget 2026 proposes to provide nearly $4 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28. This funding will support electricity infrastructure expansion, renewable energy, and priority electricity sector projects across Canada, including new funding for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program . Our electricity grids in Canada are currently far too fragmented. Stronger interties can better connect electricity systems across Canada, allowing electricity to move more easily across provincial and territorial borders. Budget 2026 proposes to provide $37 million in 2027-28 to support robust cost-benefit analysis of proposed interties and inform cross-border cost-allocation discussions. To support the allocation of investment for Canada's electricity system buildout, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $26.4 million over 10 years (on a cash basis) to Natural Resources Canada for data and modelling capacity to improve system planning and help guide investments where they will be most beneficial. Budget 2026 also proposes to provide $22.9 million over five years to Environment and Climate Change Canada to update the Clean Electricity Regulations and to develop equivalency agreements with provinces and territories where appropriate. Growing Canada's electricity system will require substantial investment. The measures above will help protect the affordability of Canada's electricity, which is important for economic growth and competitiveness. As a complement to ongoing efforts to grow Canada's electricity system in a way that safeguards affordability, Canada's new government intends to begin working with interested provinces and territories to develop new approaches to financing the largest and most transformational electricity sector projects across the infrastructure lifecycle to support our competitiveness and energy sovereignty. To improve energy reliability in the North, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $1.6 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28. This includes $713.8 million for renewable energy and capacity-building projects that help Indigenous, rural, and remote communities transition from diesel and fossil fuels to renewable energy sources, and $929.1 million to replace and upgrade aging electricity infrastructure in northern communities. This funding will support the Mayo Hydro Facility and Atlin Hydro Expansion projects . The Mayo and Atlin projects would together help strengthen the reliability of Yukon's electricity system by protecting critical existing generation capacity and bringing new power to the grid. Upgrades to the Mayo Hydro Facility would safeguard 15 megawatts of dependable hydroelectricity and help address winter blackout risks as record-breaking demand places increasing pressure on Yukon's grid. The Atlin Hydro Expansion would bring additional hydroelectricity from northern British Columbia to Yukon, with the potential to add eight megawatts of capacity to Yukon's grid and generate 31 gigawatt hours each winter, equivalent to the annual electricity use of approximately 2,500 Yukon homes. As demand for electricity grows, Canada needs new sources of reliable power that can be brought online quickly to enable investment, strengthen energy security, and support a more competitive economy. Positioning Canada at the frontier of emerging low-carbon technologies can help meet growing electricity needs while creating new opportunities for Canadian industries and workers. To realise this opportunity, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $6 billion over six years, starting in 2028-29, earmarked to support the deployment of emerging electricity generation technologies. Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) can provide efficient, reliable power to help meet the needs of growing data centres and other energy-intensive industries. Greater access to power could support the expansion of digital infrastructure in Canada, strengthening data sovereignty. SOFCs also use relatively little water, produce very low levels of conventional air pollutants, and create opportunities to build Canadian expertise and manufacturing capacity in an emerging energy technology. As electricity demand grows and Canada works to double the capacity of its grid, keeping electricity reliable and affordable will require flexibility in how power is generated. We intend to update the Clean Electricity Regulations to provide that flexibility while maintaining the goal of avoiding excessive emissions and achieving a net-zero electricity system by 2050. The proposed changes would: Allow existing electricity facilities to operate for longer, including where needed to maintain reliability. Provide more certainty for planned investments in electricity generation, as well as more flexibility, including, for example, for natural gas in the near term, as well as hybrid energy systems and distributed renewables, giving electricity systems more options to meet growing demand as the grid expands while still achieving net-zero by 2050. Make emissions reductions more cost-effective by allowing electricity producers to offset more of their emissions through verified reductions elsewhere in the sector and economy. Any changes would maintain the net-zero by 2050 goal and continue to protect the environment and human health from climate change. The proposed changes will be subject to consultation.

id: 2026|chap1-en.html|Growing Canada's nuclear advantage and powering our electricity future
section: Building a cleaner, more competitive economy
heading: Growing Canada's nuclear advantage and powering our electricity future
text: Nuclear energy is playing a growing role around the world as countries look for reliable, low-carbon electricity to meet rising demand and strengthen their energy security. Canada has a world-class nuclear sector and is well positioned to benefit from this demand, both domestically and internationally. Nuclear energy is essential to powering Canada's future. It provides non-emitting, dependable baseload power, backed by a strong domestic supply chain built on over 70 years of Canadian expertise, innovation, and intellectual property. Today, the nuclear sector is responsible for 90,000 direct and indirect jobs, and in the nuclear industry itself, 90% of jobs are in high-skilled roles. Nuclear energy contributes 13% of our national electricity supply, and it adds $22 billion to Canada's economy every year through the operation of 17 Canada Deuterium Uranium (CANDU) reactors at home and the servicing of nine reactors abroad in countries like Romania, India, and South Korea. We are committed to keeping this Canadian technology market-ready for use at home and in international markets. Global demand for nuclear energy is growing. Global nuclear investment reached approximately $88 billion in 2023 and is projected to reach between $94 billion and $202 billion annually by 2030. At least 30 countries are pursuing their first nuclear builds, creating a significant opportunity for Canadian companies. Canada is well positioned to compete for that investment. Homegrown CANDU technology is part of the opportunity, but Canadian manufacturers and service providers also have capabilities that support other reactor technologies, giving Canada a role in nuclear projects regardless of the technology selected. Canada also has the tools to help its nuclear industry compete internationally. Export Development Canada offers financing, insurance, and risk-management products to help Canadian companies expand abroad, complementing Canada's technology, manufacturing, and service expertise. In June 2026, we presented the Nuclear Energy Strategy for Canada , setting out a plan to grow the sector by unlocking investment, modernising regulation, strengthening Canadian research and development, and promoting Canadian nuclear expertise abroad. To implement key commitments under the Strategy, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $518.5 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, and $18.1 million ongoing to advance Canada's nuclear research, supply chains, workforce, and regulatory capacity. This includes: $261 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, and $14 million ongoing, to Natural Resources Canada to develop nuclear supply chains, support research and development, and advance research reactor capacity and readiness. $127 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, and $1 million ongoing, to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited for research infrastructure, research and development, workforce development, and other strategic nuclear capabilities. $131.1 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) to prepare for new nuclear projects and become the sole federal regulator for nuclear energy projects. Of this amount, $18.3 million would be cost-recovered. $14.4 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, and $3.1 million ongoing, to Global Affairs Canada, for nuclear export promotion and government-to-government engagement. $3.3 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to Health Canada to support the CNSC with expertise on the human health impacts of radiation exposure. We have already taken significant steps to finance new nuclear projects, including up to $2 billion from the Canada Growth Fund for the Darlington Nuclear Project, alongside support for Indigenous participation through the Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program ; $970 million in low-interest financing from the Canada Infrastructure Bank; and access to the refundable Clean Electricity investment tax credit . Export financing for up to $3 billion has also been made available, through Export Development Canada , for the construction of two new CANDU reactors in Romania. The Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program , alongside Ontario through its Indigenous Opportunities Financing Program, will provide an approximately $715 million loan guarantee to allow seven First Nations in Ontario to own a significant minority interest in the Darlington New Nuclear Project. This transaction represents the largest Indigenous loan guarantee ever issued in Canada and one of the largest Indigenous investments in a major infrastructure project in Canadian history.

section: Building a cleaner, more competitive economy
heading: Expanding Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure
text: As more Canadians choose zero-emission vehicles, demand for electric vehicle chargers will continue to grow. Within five years, EV sales are projected to reach nearly 40% of global car sales. We have invested steadily to expand the charging network by supporting more than 50,000 chargers to date. A larger network makes it easier and more convenient for Canadians to drive electric vehicles, particularly in rural communities, helping Canada become a global leader in vehicle electrification. Budget 2026 builds on this progress achieved, with the ambition to roughly double the number of federally supported chargers, making it easier for Canadian drivers to save money, plan their routes, and travel in confidence: To support the installation of over 55,000 additional EV chargers in areas where the infrastructure is needed most, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $587 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to Environment and Climate Change Canada to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program . To fund research and development for charging infrastructure, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $45 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to Natural Resources Canada. This funding would help bring innovative Canadian EV charging solutions to market, delivering more affordable, reliable, and accessible EV charging solutions that work for Canadians, businesses, and the electricity grid. To support the transition of the federal fleet to zero-emission vehicles, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $2.2 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to renew the Greening Government Operations Fleet Program , which conducts readiness assessments to support the transition of the federal vehicle fleet to zero-emission vehicles.

id: 2026|chap1-en.html|Bringing critical minerals from mine to market
section: Unlocking the full potential of Canada's natural resources
heading: Bringing critical minerals from mine to market
text: Canada stands as a global leader in mining and critical minerals, such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, and rare earth elements that are used in batteries, electric vehicles, and other clean technologies. We are known around the world for our mining schools, for our expertise and technology, and for the reliability we offer as a mining nation. But for too long, Canada has fallen behind in bringing those minerals from mine to market. That is why we are focused on increasing Canadian production and processing of our minerals. That work includes strengthening the domestic supply chains that bring these minerals from mine to market. By working with Indigenous partners, industry, and international allies to responsibly develop more resource opportunities in Canada, we are creating good jobs and increasing our resource sovereignty. Critical minerals projects valued at over $44.6 billion were under construction or had completed the Impact Assessment or Environmental Assessment processes as of 2025, as well as select 2026 projects (Figure 1.10). In the past year, Canada has signed over 50 critical minerals agreements with more than 15 countries, unlocking $20 billion in investment while reducing our reliance on foreign supply chains (Figure 1.11). In July 2026, we announced the launch of the $2 billion Canada Critical Minerals Accelerator (CCMA). Delivered by Export Development Canada, the CCMA helps move priority critical mineral projects forward, allowing us to invest alongside industry in projects that strengthen Canada's supply of minerals needed for technologies such as batteries, semiconductors, and defence equipment. Canada announced its first agreement under the CCMA in support of Teck Resources' $850 million expansion of its Trail Operations in British Columbia, alongside a $400 million investment from the Canada Growth Fund announced this summer. To build on this progress and unlock more of Canada's critical minerals potential, Budget 2026 proposes to: Renew the Canadian Critical Minerals Strategy , which supports strategic investments in the technology needed to mine and process our critical minerals, expands our geoscience and research capacity, provides targeted funding for priority critical minerals projects, and keeps government priorities aligned with market needs. Budget 2026 proposes to provide Natural Resources Canada with $424.4 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, to support this renewal. Extend the Mineral Exploration Tax Credit and Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit for an additional five years, until March 31, 2032. Budget 2026 also proposes to expand the Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit to include antimony. These measures are expected to provide $956 million in support of mineral exploration investment over five years, starting in 2026-27. Align the tax treatment of helium exploration and development expenditures, as well as expenditures incurred to acquire helium resource properties, with that of the conventional oil and gas sector. This change would also allow helium companies to benefit more from the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction , allowing them to immediately expense more capital investments in the helium sector. These amendments would apply to expenses incurred on or after Budget Day and are expected to provide tax relief of $54 million over four years, starting in 2027-28. Chart 1.5 presents the policy approaches of nine countries across five key dimensions: strategic clarity, delivery architecture, funding and de-risking, evidence of execution, and sovereign capability. This analysis from a recent report (PwC's Mine 2026: Ambition to Action ) finds that Canada is positioned as a global leader in critical minerals policy.

section: Unlocking the full potential of Canada's natural resources
heading: Strengthening Canada's forest sector
text: Canada has a world-renowned forest sector. It is the bedrock of hundreds of rural, remote, and Indigenous communities, employs nearly 200,000 workers, and is a staple of Canadian resource exports. In 2025, the sector contributed $29.7 billion to Canada's GDP. Due to unjustified U.S. tariffs, changing global markets, and shifting wood product needs, our forest sector is facing significant pressures. The sector must improve its productivity and competitiveness to keep pace. That is why we are supporting and strengthening Canada's forest industry for the challenges of today and the demands of the future in Budget 2026. It proposes: $500 million over six years, starting in 2027-28, to Natural Resources Canada, to strengthen fibre supply chains and support provinces, territories, Indigenous partners, and industry in advancing forest management and stewardship, and deploying new technologies and practices. $2 billion over six years, starting in 2027-28, to Natural Resources Canada to help businesses in the forest sector modernise facilities and equipment, improve productivity, and expand production of higher-value products, as well as to support research, development, and demonstration projects. $4 billion over six years, starting in 2027-28, on a cash basis, to Export Development Canada through the Canada Account to support a new Forestry Sector Accelerator to make investments in new large-scale facilities and in major transformations of existing facilities, including biorefineries, biofuel facilities, and other facilities producing higher-value and innovative forest products.
