heading: Advancing Canada's climate competitiveness
text: As global demand grows for clean technologies, low-carbon products, and sustainable solutions, Canada has an opportunity to contribute to emissions reductions at home and abroad while generating significant economic benefits. By lowering the carbon intensity of our exports, we can help reach global climate objectives while increasing their competitiveness abroad. Furthermore, by providing certainty on emissions policy, we can help businesses and clean technology developers have greater confidence in their operations as we continue to build a low-carbon future. Last year, we established a framework to help with this transition: driving investment, encouraging innovation, and reducing Canada's emissions over time while maintaining Canada's competitiveness. This pragmatic approach provides businesses with greater certainty as they make long-term investment decisions; it also helps ensure Canada remains an attractive place to invest, grow a business, and create good, well-paying jobs. To support the continued transition to a low-carbon economy, we are: Working to establish a predictable and effective carbon pricing system that supports emissions reductions while providing clarity for businesses and investors. As part of this effort, we intend to update the federal industrial carbon pricing benchmark to provide greater certainty for industrial emitters, clean technology developers, and capital markets, and to support continued investment in emissions reductions. Collaborating with provinces and territories to explore opportunities for ensuring greater alignment and linkages between carbon markets across Canada, improving market efficiency, and helping achieve emissions reductions at lower cost. Amending the Clean Electricity Regulations to provide greater flexibility while maintaining the goal of net-zero by 2050 and updating vehicle greenhouse gas emissions standards to reflect changes in consumer demand and advances in vehicle technology. To further help Canadian businesses and industries adopt energy-saving technologies and reduce emissions: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $400 million over seven years, starting in 2027-28, to Environment and Climate Change Canada to support the renewal of the Green Industrial Facilities and Manufacturing Program, now named the Strategic High-efficiency Industrial Facilities Transition (SHIFT). SHIFT will de-risk projects and accelerate adoption of energy-saving technologies at industrial and manufacturing facilities, including small- and medium-sized enterprises. To help young Canadians shape Canada's transition to a low-carbon economy, the Youth Climate Corps , led by Employment and Social Development Canada, Natural Resources Canada, and Parks Canada, will help more than 2,000 young people gain the skills and experience needed for careers in climate-related and emergency management fields, strengthening Canada's workforce and supporting a clean, low-carbon, and resilient future.

heading: Mobilising sustainable investment
text: As global demand for low-carbon goods and technologies grows, Canada is taking steps to help attract investment in the industries and projects that will drive future economic growth. Work is underway on the independently developed Made-in-Canada sustainable investment guidelines that will help direct investment toward low-carbon projects, with draft criteria for the electricity, transportation, and buildings sectors expected by the end of 2026. In addition, Budget 2026 proposes to: Develop a new Sustainable Bond Framework for government issuance, using the Made-in-Canada sustainable investment guidelines. This framework will be prepared by the Department of Finance Canada. Showcase progress on the Made-in-Canada sustainable investment guidelines and connect investors with new opportunities through a Sustainable Finance Conference that the Canadian Climate Institute will host in February 2027. We also continue to advance disclosure requirements for environmental, social, and governance considerations, including climate-related risks, for federally regulated pension plans. These form part of a broader initiative to improve the transparency and governance of these plans. We also continue to engage provinces and territories on supporting voluntary climate disclosures across the economy. Clear and comparable climate disclosures help firms access new markets, strengthen business resilience and investor confidence, and remain competitive in the face of growing reporting expectations from customers and investors at home and abroad.

heading: Advancing the Whole-of-Government Competition Plan
text: Building on the momentum from recent reforms, in the 2026 Spring Economic Update, we launched the Whole-of-Government Competition Plan , which expands Canada's competition agenda beyond individual sectors so that all government decision-making falls under a pro-competition lens. Through these efforts, we are reviewing federal policies, regulations, and programs to identify what unnecessarily limits competition while preserving important public policy objectives. The Competition Plan is advancing work across several areas: Cutting red tape to open markets: Initial reforms include several competition-enhancing measures identified through the Red Tape Review . Many of these are advancing through the Cutting Red Tape for All Canadians Act , while others are expected to be implemented by departments within the next 12 months. The Competition Plan will identify outdated or unnecessary rules that make it harder for new businesses to enter markets, existing businesses to grow and innovate, and Canadians to benefit from more choice and better value. This work will inform further regulatory reforms to strengthen competition. Opening federal contracts to more businesses: Public Services and Procurement Canada and the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat are simplifying procurement rules, reducing paperwork, and improving transparency so that small- and medium-sized businesses can more easily compete for federal contracts. The Small Business Procurement Program will better align procurement regulations, helping bring more suppliers to the table, strengthen competition, and give Canadian businesses more opportunities to grow, while supporting broader procurement objectives, including the Buy Canadian Policy . Designing business supports to promote competition: We are reviewing how federal business support programs can give new and growing firms a fairer chance to compete, while keeping funding focused on its economic objectives. This will examine whether program rules make it easier—or harder—for businesses to enter markets, grow, and challenge established players. The findings will help improve program design and develop an approach that can be applied more broadly across federal business support programs over time. As part of this work: Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to assess and integrate competition considerations into federal business support programs, starting with the Strategic Response Fund . A Cabinet Directive on regulatory competitiveness: The federal Cabinet will ensure new regulations and the broader regulatory system are examined through a competitiveness, growth, and investment lens. The Cabinet Directive on Regulatory Competitiveness and Red Tape Reduction will help Canada advance a world-class regulatory system that protects the public interest while providing the efficiency and clarity needed for Canada to attract investment, support innovation, and strengthen Canada's long-term competitiveness. The Whole-of-Government Competition Plan is also advancing measures to strengthen competition, attract investment, and expand consumer choice across the Canadian economy. We will advance measures within federal jurisdiction and work with provinces and territories where coordinated action is required. Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to: Make it easier for consumers to switch providers: Expand data portability rights to additional sectors, including telecommunications and air transportation. These rights would be implemented following the establishment of the new data portability framework under the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act , making it easier for Canadians to switch telecommunications providers and securely reuse their information when choosing different services. Strengthen Competition Bureau investigations: Make it easier for federal institutions to share relevant information with the Competition Bureau when it is investigating possible anti-competitive conduct, by formally recognising the Bureau as an investigative body under the Privacy Regulations . Information sharing would remain subject to the same legal limits and privacy protections that apply to other investigative bodies. Address restrictions on lower prices: Consult on potential reforms to address practices that prevent retailers from offering or advertising lower prices, such as suppliers pressuring stores not to discount products below a set price. The consultation would consider options to strengthen the Competition Bureau's ability to act when these practices limit price competition and make it harder for Canadians to find better deals. Remove anti-competitive property controls : Work with provinces and territories to end anti-competitive property controls that restrict competition in the retail grocery sector, building on Manitoba's new model for restrictions. Limit non-compete agreements: Work with provinces and territories to expand restrictions on non-compete agreements in employment contracts across Canada toward harmonised restrictions modelled on the federal approach. To prevent new government initiatives from creating unnecessary barriers to competition, we are also embedding competition considerations into federal decision-making. As part of the Cabinet Directive on Regulatory Competitiveness and Red Tape Reduction , the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat will integrate competitiveness impact assessment into the regulatory development process, while the Department of Finance Canada will do the same for budget and Cabinet decision-making. Each department will provide guidance and oversight in its area, with implementation targeted for winter 2027. The Whole-of-Government Competition Plan , together with efforts to lower internal trade barriers, establishes a broad and ambitious agenda to strengthen competition across the economy and ensure pro-competitive policies are prioritised across government. Key elements of the Competition Plan and actions taken since 2025 to advance a more competitive Canadian economy are highlighted below. Competition by default: Modernising the federal rules, programs, and institutions that shape markets, and ensuring government decisions promote competition. Apply a competition lens to new regulations and policies • Strengthen the Competition Bureau's tools and investigative powers • Reinforce competition objectives in federal regulatory oversight Make it easier for businesses to enter markets, compete on a level playing field, and grow by reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens, facilitating entry, and improving access to infrastructure and key inputs. Reduce red tape Improve access to essential infrastructure and networks in the telecom sector Facilitate entry and growth in the financial sector by streamlining entry processes and modernising regulatory frameworks Engage provinces and territories to support labour mobility in all sectors of Canada's economy Give Canadians the information and freedom to choose the provider that offers the best value by making prices easier to understand and compare, reducing switching costs and lock-in, and enhancing consumer protection. Improve transparency of total banking fees charged annually to make it easier for Canadians to compare offerings, including through improved data sharing via consumer-driven banking Make comparison and switching easier across telecom plans and enhance consumer protection across telecom services Increase transparency in pricing, including in the insured mortgage market Engage provinces and territories on restricting property controls in the retail grocery sector Take action against surveillance pricing by modernising privacy legislation Give new ideas and business models room to test products and commercialise technology through modernised market rules and greater access to data and infrastructure. Establish regulatory frameworks to facilitate innovative financial products and technologies Release more high-quality spectrum Enable investment in high-quality telecommunications networks Expand data portability beyond consumer-driven banking to other sectors to support innovation and consumer choice Competition that delivers More choice. Lower prices. Stronger growth. For Canadians: more transparent prices, more choice, lower switching costs, and fewer excessive fees. For businesses: easier entry, fairer opportunities to compete, and more room to scale. For the economy: stronger investment and innovation, higher productivity, greater affordability, and a more resilient Canadian market.

heading: Increasing competition in the telecommunications sector
text: Fast, reliable, and affordable Internet and cellular services are essential to how Canadians work, learn, run their businesses, and stay connected. Yet too many Canadians, particularly in rural and remote communities, still face gaps in coverage and reliability. While wireless prices have fallen, with the price of a 60 GB mobile plan falling from an average of $105 in 2022 to being widely available in the $40 to $50 range, Canadians continue to face limited choice, confusing offers, and barriers to switching providers. To increase competition, affordability, and transparency for consumers, in October 2026 we published the Telecommunications Competition Roadmap announced in the 2026 Spring Economic Update. It sets out a coordinated plan to strengthen competition and affordability across Canada, while enabling investment in network infrastructure to support emerging technologies and data traffic growth. This marks the first time a federal government has set out a comprehensive telecom competition agenda covering everything from broad policy to specific regulatory actions. Once implemented, the Roadmap will: Expand competition across the economy: Competitors need fair access to the infrastructure required to serve Canadians. The government and the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission are advancing measures to help providers expand, including by finalising wholesale Internet rates, improving access to wireless networks, accelerating regulatory decisions, and resolving access disputes more quickly. New "dig-once" and tower-siting approaches will also lower construction costs and speed up network deployment. Help Canadians find better prices: Competition works best when Canadians can easily compare offers and switch providers. The Roadmap builds on new rules that eliminate fees to activate, change, or cancel a plan. It is expected to save consumers approximately $100 million each year. It will also promote more affordable plans, ensure transparency when shopping for Internet offers, simplify consumer protection rules, and improve awareness of the independent complaints process. Build stronger, more innovative networks: Canada also needs sustained investment in high-quality networks that reach every region. We will release more spectrum for 5G and private networks, support satellite services that can extend coverage in rural and remote areas, update spectrum transfer rules, and advance new infrastructure models that improve access for competition and significantly enhance investments in our national telecom network infrastructure. These actions will support better coverage, faster services, and greater choice for Canadians, while strengthening the underlying digital infrastructure that businesses need to grow.

heading: Increasing competition in the financial sector
text: Canada offers an attractive world-renowned capital environment, and the financial sector is integral to getting projects financed, growing our economy, and building Canada Strong. At the same time, it would benefit from being a more competitive market. Budget 2026 builds on the government's existing reforms to improve Canada's financial sector. These measures, including consumer-driven banking and payments, will facilitate market entry, support firms as they grow and scale, and modernise regulatory and supervisory frameworks. For Canadians, this means more choice, lower prices, and greater access to innovative financial services. For businesses, it means better access to the financing they need to invest, grow, and create jobs here in Canada. In a rapidly changing world, financial sector regulation must adapt and respond to evolving technologies, business models, and consumer needs. Canada is acting to ensure competition plays a greater role in how the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) regulates. OSFI supervises federally regulated financial institutions, including banks, insurers, trust and loan companies, and federal credit unions. We are modernising how OSFI regulates and supervises these institutions as we maintain confidence in the reliability and resilience of Canada's financial system. Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to: Introduce a secondary competition objective for OSFI through amendments to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act . This will help ensure that competition considerations, such as proportionality, compliance burden, and market impacts, are more clearly and consistently reflected in how OSFI regulates and supervises financial institutions. Canada has a stable, world-class financial sector. At the same time, it is important to attract more entrants and help them expand to improve products and services while lowering prices for consumers. Responsibly modernising the financial sector is a key part of the government's commitment to make life more affordable for Canadians. To that end, Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to: Make the process for becoming a federally regulated financial institution more predictable, transparent, and timely by amending the Bank Act , Trust and Loan Companies Act , and Insurance Companies Act to establish a one-year timeline for making decisions on applications by new entrants. Expand exit options for deposit-taking institutions by amending the Bank Act and Trust and Loan Companies Act to allow for more flexibility to transfer assets and liabilities to other financial institutions. This will make it easier for solvent but troubled financial institutions to pursue private market solutions, while protecting depositors and helping consumers avoid costly service disruptions. Encourage the entry and growth of mid-sized challenger banks by amending the Bank Act to permit greater flexibility on ownership structures. This will be achieved by exempting foreign bank subsidiaries with less than $8 billion in equity from the public holding requirement, provided that their foreign parent is widely held and listed on a recognised foreign stock exchange, and raising the threshold at which banks must transition to widely held ownership from $12 billion to $25 billion in equity. Provide greater clarity and predictability for new and growing financial institutions through a policy statement issued by the Minister of Finance. The statement will provide guidance on how ministerial tools may be used to support the entry of federally regulated financial institutions, including credit union continuance, and promote a more proportionate and competition-supportive financial institutions framework. Make it easier for federal credit unions to access capital and pursue growth opportunities by amending the Bank Act to provide greater flexibility for qualifying cooperative shareholders to invest in and control a federal credit union. These changes will help credit unions expand their reach and serve more Canadians and businesses. To build a stronger Canada and be masters of our destiny , Canadians need access to reliable funding to plan for the future. It helps households finance the major purchases they make and gives businesses the capital they need to compete and win. Expanding funding opportunities will allow smaller institutions to expand into new markets, provide more mortgages and support business investment, and compete more effectively on pricing, products, and services. At the same time, stronger depositor protections will help Canadians safeguard more of their savings and support greater competition for deposits. To support these objectives, Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to: Modernise the deposit insurance framework by amending the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act , including to increase the deposit insurance limit to $250,000, provide temporary high-balance coverage for certain life events, such as the sale of a home, and remove the limit for eligible deposits in registered and tax-free accounts. Work with small- and medium-sized deposit-taking institutions to better understand their funding needs and explore options to strengthen access to stable, cost-effective funding that supports growth, competition, and innovation. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) is an independent federal agency responsible for the regulation and supervision of federally regulated financial institutions and pension plans. As an important part of the federal financial safety net, OSFI contributes to public confidence in the Canadian financial system. As part of its broader modernisation agenda, OSFI is taking steps to make Canada's regulatory framework more transparent, proportionate, and responsive while maintaining resilience. Current initiatives include: Adjusting the capital framework and adapting prudential frameworks for small- and medium-sized deposit-taking institutions to better reflect their activities and risk profile, strengthening their ability to compete. Making targeted capital adjustments across federally regulated financial institutions that improve risk sensitivity and support sustainable economic growth while maintaining resilience. These initiatives build on recent reforms to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden, streamline approvals, and ensure requirements are proportionate to the size and risk profile of institutions, helping support entry, growth, and competition in Canada's financial sector. Recent measures include OSFI's Streamlined Approvals Framework for Targeted New Entrants, a modernised Supervisory Framework, and the consolidation of more than 600 pages of guidance. Notably, OSFI has also lowered the Domestic Stability Buffer, an additional capital cushion that Canada's largest banks are required to hold to help absorb losses during periods of stress. This measured adjustment reflects the sustained strength and resilience of Canada's domestic systemically important banks and frees up capital that can be deployed in support of the Canadian economy. These measures, along with the government's proposed changes to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act , will help create a more open, competitive, and innovative banking sector, improve affordability and choice for consumers and businesses, and strengthen the conditions for long-term economic growth.

heading: Unlocking infrastructure investment and economic growth
text: As we work to unlock the infrastructure investment and economic growth needed to get big things built at scale and speed, we know that access to long-term private capital is integral. We are taking action to expand infrastructure investment opportunities for Canadian life insurers to increase the capital available to Canadians. Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to: Expand infrastructure investment opportunities for Canadian life insurers by amending the Insurance Companies Act and the Investments in Permitted Infrastructure Entities Regulations to broaden the scope of permitted infrastructure investments. This will unlock additional capital that can be invested over the long term for infrastructure projects and support the construction of transportation networks, energy infrastructure, and other assets that strengthen Canada's economy, creating high-paying careers for Canadians.

id: 2026|chap1-en.html|Advancing the digital transformation of the financial system
heading: Advancing the digital transformation of the financial system
text: From the applications they choose, to buying Canadian at the grocery store, to picking where they vacation—Canadians are ensuring that we are our own best customer. As Canadians increasingly choose Canada, we are making sure that money can move quickly, safely, and conveniently. Modern payment systems are integral to a stronger and more resilient economy. Budget 2026 builds on significant progress to modernise Canada's payment ecosystem, including establishing a regulatory framework for payment service providers, expanding access to Payments Canada's systems, and supporting the launch of a new fast-payment system called the Real-Time Rail on November 9, 2026, which will enable individuals and businesses to send and receive data-rich payments instantly, with immediate access to funds. These efforts complement other initiatives underway to advance consumer-driven banking, establish Canada's stablecoin framework, and combat financial fraud. Building on these foundational reforms, Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to: Launch the next phase of Canada's payments modernisation, guided by a public consultation expected in early 2027 on future priorities and the statutory review of the Canadian Payments Act . Strengthen the Bank of Canada's oversight of payment service providers through targeted amendments to the Retail Payment Activities Act. Work with provinces and territories to develop harmonised consumer protection requirements for payment service providers regulated under the Retail Payment Activities Act. Develop a pilot project for the use of voluntary digital credentials in financial services to support innovation and help combat identity fraud. The project would be developed by the Canadian Digital Service in collaboration with the Department of Finance Canada. Collectively, these initiatives will help maximise the benefits of recent reforms, strengthen consumer protection, improve the governance and stewardship of Canada's payments infrastructure, and harness emerging technologies to deliver safer, more affordable financial services for Canadians and businesses. We have also enacted the Stablecoin Act . With the Stablecoin Act , Canadians have a safer and more reliable way to make digital payments. The Act offers opportunities for faster and more efficient transactions, a broader range of payment options, and increased competition and innovation. At the same time, it introduces appropriate safeguards to protect consumers and maintain confidence in stablecoins. Alongside ongoing consultations on the proposed regulations under the Stablecoin Act , we are continuing to strengthen Canada's stablecoin framework by providing greater regulatory clarity and advancing work to strengthen consumer protections. To that end, Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to: Require federally regulated financial institutions to issue stablecoins through non-financial institution subsidiaries regulated under the Stablecoin Act and extend the Stablecoin Act to foreign financial institutions that are not prudentially regulated in Canada, to promote consistent regulatory treatment across stablecoin issuers. Continue to engage with stakeholders on options to strengthen consumer protections in the event of stablecoin issuer or custodian insolvency, while supporting responsible innovation in the stablecoin market. Budget 2026 will help expand access to skills and economic opportunities as Canada builds a more clean and competitive economy, by: Expanding access to reliable, clean electricity with measures under the National Electricity Strategy , while reducing greenhouse gas emissions and contributing to long-term health and environmental benefits. These investments will also support skilled jobs and help create new opportunities for northern, remote, and Indigenous communities, supporting broader participation in the clean energy economy. Strengthening Canada's forest sector to support employment and economic opportunities in rural, remote, and Indigenous communities, particularly where the forest sector is a major source of jobs and economic activity. Indigenous Peoples and communities would benefit from enhanced opportunities to participate in forest stewardship, business development, and economic growth, helping build stronger local economies and more resilient forest-dependent communities. Expanding access to EV charging infrastructure, the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program supports new economic opportunities in the growing zero-emission vehicle sector, including jobs and skills related to the deployment, operation, and maintenance of clean transportation infrastructure. Further information on the expected gender and diversity impacts of Budget 2026 measures across a range of population groups is provided in Annex 4.

chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Building a stronger, more sovereign economy
heading: Moving major projects forward faster
text: For too long, nation-building infrastructure in Canada was bogged down in red tape, leaving enormous investments on the table. The path to approval was confusing and overlapping, and the onus was on the proponent to navigate the system. In August 2025, Canada's new government changed that by establishing the Major Projects Office to streamline and accelerate regulatory approval processes and help structure and coordinate project financing. The Major Projects Office is working. Canada is working. Since September 2025, 28 nation-building initiatives have been referred to the Major Projects Office that position Canada for growth in broad sectors like electricity, nuclear energy, liquefied natural gas, critical minerals, and transportation infrastructure. The Office is doing this in full partnership with Indigenous Peoples, and while protecting the environment. The 18 projects referred to the Major Projects Office have clear proponents and require federal coordination and support to succeed; collectively, these represent more than $194 billion in new investments, estimated to support 200,000 jobs per year during the construction phase. The 10 transformative strategies are early-stage initiatives that would strengthen Canada's economy. To advance these efforts, we introduced Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act , in September 2026. It establishes a "one project, one decision, one year" approach to federal approvals. Consultations will be coordinated through a single federal process, reducing duplication and consultation fatigue while supporting more meaningful, rights-based dialogue. That is how we get projects built faster and strengthen Canada's trade corridors and ports, supporting our workers in Canada's federally regulated sectors. Our plan gives Canada one of the most streamlined and predictable major project approval processes among peer economies. It keeps us a country of high standards, one that is committed to consultation and upholding Indigenous rights. The new timelines do not change section 35 rights, the duty to consult, or treaty obligations. Faster decisions will come from better federal coordination and less duplication. Speed, certainty, and predictability are, themselves, competitive advantages. With these reforms, Canada can once again get big things built, for all Canadians. Budget 2026 proposes to establish a major projects management entity to ensure approved projects can access the expertise and resources required to move quickly. This purpose-built organisation would have specialised technical and project development expertise to support certain projects, manage risks, and keep them on track. Budget 2026 proposes to provide $187.4 million over five years, beginning in 2026-27, and $24.2 million in future years to launch and operate a major projects management entity and begin support for the Mackenzie Valley Highway and the Taltson Hydro Expansion project. Our plan is working and delivering projects at generational speed. With the Major Projects Office and new measures in Budget 2026, we are creating a faster, more efficient, and more predictable system for building Canada Strong. The proposed Act would strengthen Canada's ability to build major projects, move goods, and support workers Faster project reviews and decisions Target federal reviews and decisions within one year once a comprehensive application is submitted. Advance a "one project, one decision, one year" approach to reduce duplication across federal reviews and permits. Better coordinate assessments, permitting, and consultation through a lead federal assessor. Clarify lead roles for the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada , the Canada Energy Regulator , and the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission , depending on project type. Establish a Crown Consultation Hub to help coordinate consultation with Indigenous Peoples. Maintain environmental protections and uphold Indigenous rights. Trade corridors, ports, and transportation Formally designate strategic trade corridors . Create a Transportation Projects Office to coordinate federal approvals for priority transportation projects. Remove bottlenecks and support more predictable federal processes for transportation projects. Modernise port governance and transportation rules. Reduce administrative burdens and expand digital trade processes . Strengthen supply chains and help Canadian goods reach more markets efficiently. Worker protections and labour relations in federally regulated industries Modernise the Canada Labour Code to support earlier bargaining, negotiated settlements, and dispute resolution while fully protecting the right to strike . Update federal labour protections to reflect a changing economy. Increase prevention activities, inspection capacity, and enforcement to improve workplace safety. Add 26 Canada Industrial Relations Board staff to help reduce backlogs of complaints by workers against employers. Strengthen enforcement against worker misclassification and wage theft . The Act is intended to provide greater speed, certainty, and predictability for major projects, strengthen trade infrastructure, and support workers while maintaining environmental protections and upholding Indigenous rights. As we continue to move major projects forward faster, we are supporting projects at different stages of development. Projects referred to the Major Projects Office benefit from dedicated federal coordination and support. Those later listed as projects of national interest benefit from a streamlined federal approval process offering greater certainty and advancing them even faster. For example, in October 2026, the Pacific Link and Roberts Bank Terminal 2 were listed as projects of national interest under the Building Canada Act . The government is taking a balanced approach to growing Canada's energy sector while lowering its emissions. Pacific Link, a new pipeline to the West Coast, is now a project of national interest, while the Pathways Project would reduce emissions through large-scale carbon capture and storage infrastructure. Together, these projects would: Expand market access , with Pacific Link providing capacity to transport one million barrels per day to the West Coast and expanding access to international markets for Canadian energy products. Increase the value of Canada's resources by enabling greater access to premium prices in growing Asian markets and helping to reduce the price discount on Canadian oil relative to U.S. oil. Reduce emissions , with the Pathways Project and other emissions reduction commitments from the Oil Sands Alliance, achieving 16 million tonnes of emissions reductions per year. Support investment and long-term economic growth , creating high-paying new jobs while lowering the emissions intensity of Canadian oil production. On August 17, 2026, the Labrador Trough Clean Power, Critical Minerals and Infrastructure Corridor was referred to the Major Projects Office. This transformative strategy unlocks the Labrador Trough's full economic potential, harnessing the region's clean, hydroelectric power and high-purity iron ore while building the necessary transmission lines to realise the region's true economic potential. The Major Projects Office will coordinate and structure federal financing, accelerate permitting requirements, and work with Indigenous Peoples, including the Innu people, to forge meaningful partnerships. The Labrador Trough, stretching across Newfoundland and Labrador and Québec, is a world-class mining region with significant hydroelectric capability and high-purity iron ore. To harness this strategic asset and create high-paying careers for Canadian workers, the government announced the referral of the Labrador Trough Clean Power, Critical Minerals and Infrastructure Corridor to the Major Projects Office. When complete, Labrador Trough will represent the largest clean investment in North American history. This development would: Expand clean electricity generation , through the expansion of Churchill Falls and development of Gull Island, creating 14,000 megawatts of clean, renewable power and nearly tripling Churchill Falls' current generating capacity; Increase transmission capacity , through new transmission infrastructure to deliver electricity to the Labrador Trough; Unlock mining and industrial development , by increasing clean power capacity in the region; and Support low-carbon growth , by helping Canada produce the electricity needed to double its capacity by 2050 and increasing the supply of high-purity iron ore for low-carbon steel supply chains. With Canada positioned to become the leading supplier of clean and conventional energy, both to ourselves and to the world, projects like Pacific Link and strategies like the Labrador Trough Clean Power, Critical Minerals and Infrastructure Corridor prove the benefits of the national, collaborative approach laid out in the Building Canada Act . Since July 2026, the Major Projects Office has been assessing three additional potential projects of national interest alongside consultations with Indigenous communities and provincial and territorial governments (see Figures 2.3 – 2.7). Among those three projects is the Mackenzie Valley Highway, which will create a new all-season economic corridor in the Northwest Territories connecting Wrigley to Inuvik. The Highway will provide year-round connectivity to nearly 2,000 residents in the three currently isolated communities of Norman Wells, Tulita, and Fort Good Hope and give the nearly 6,000 residents of the Beaufort Delta a 1,200 km shorter route to Yellowknife. The communities of Colville Lake and Deline will also benefit from shorter winter road construction and more reliable travel windows. To unlock this economic corridor: Budget 2026 proposes to fully fund the construction and certain maintenance costs of the Mackenzie Valley Highway. Listed as a project of national interest under Schedule 1 of the Building Canada Act on October 1, 2026. Development: 1,250 km pipeline from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deep-water port near Delta, British Columbia. Capacity: The proposed pipeline would transport one million barrels per day of Canadian crude oil. Economic impact: Will create up to 140,000 jobs across the country and generate over $20 billion in GDP per year. Indigenous participation: Offer of a minimum of 10% ownership interest in the project and employment, training, contracting, and procurement opportunities. Listed as a project of national interest under Schedule 1 of the Building Canada Act on October 30, 2026. Location: Delta, British Columbia Port capacity: The proposed three-berth marine container terminal would add 2.4 million twenty-foot equivalent units of annual container capacity, increasing the Port of Vancouver's container-handling capacity by approximately 50%. Economic impact: Over $100 billion in annual trade capacity enabled, over $3 billion in projected annual GDP contribution, and over 17,000 projected ongoing supply-chain jobs. Trade diversification: Will support Canada's growth and trade diversification objectives, including doubling exports to non-U.S. markets by 2035. Indigenous partnerships: 27 First Nations have signed Mutual Benefit Agreements with the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority. Began consultations with Indigenous communities and the Government of Ontario in July 2026, as part of the process to assess its potential listing as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act . Sustainable: Will replace interim storage in facilities at reactor sites. International best practice: Canada's plan for the safe long-term management of used nuclear fuel is consistent with best practices adopted by other countries. Safety: Canada's plan will protect people and the environment for generations to come. Funding: Funded by the owners of used nuclear fuel. Currently under consideration for listing as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act . 230 km road supporting a deep-water port and airstrip. Moving Canada's critical minerals to export markets. Inuit owned and led resources company , developing the Kitikmeot for the benefit of the Kitikmeot Inuit. Construction start: Targeted for late 2029. In Nunavut, the project will support 572 jobs annually during construction and 239 during operations. Induced mining projects could result in a further 6,800 jobs during construction and 4,900 jobs annually once operational. In addition to projects being considered for listing under the Building Canada Act, we are advancing a broader portfolio of nation-building projects through funding, coordination, and support from the Major Projects Office. A few of these projects are already well underway. These include: LNG Canada Phase 2, Kitimat, British Columbia: In September 2026, LNG Canada began construction on the Phase 2 expansion of its site in Kitimat, which will double its production capacity to a total of 28 million tonnes of LNG per year. This project will provide employment opportunities in local communities, including around 6,000 direct construction jobs, and up to 240 operations jobs across the LNG plant and the Coastal GasLink pipeline. Contrecoeur Terminal Container Project, Contrecoeur, Québec: In August 2026, the Montreal Port Authority announced the start of in-water construction work for the Contrecoeur Expansion Project, marking the beginning of a major new construction phase for the future container terminal. This will support up to 8,000 direct and indirect jobs during construction. Red Chris Mine extension, northwestern British Columbia: In July 2026, we announced a federal contribution of $500 million to support the Red Chris Mine extension, which will increase Canada's annual copper production by more than 15% while reducing greenhouse gas emissions by more than 70%. This project will employ roughly 1,500 workers during operation, with a peak of approximately 1,800 workers during construction. Nouveau Monde Graphite's Matawinie Mine : In May 2026, the Government of Canada and Nouveau Monde Graphite announced the start of construction on the Matawinie Mine in Saint-Michel-des-Saints, Québec, which will be the largest graphite mine in North America and in the G7. Together with the planned active anode material plant, this project will become a vital part of Canada's first integrated graphite operation and bolster the emerging battery hub in Bécancour, Québec, employing over 1,000 people during construction. Ensuring that Indigenous communities can fully participate in, and benefit from, the major projects shaping Canada's future is an important step toward economic reconciliation. Indigenous participation in major projects can create generational wealth and long-term prosperity, supporting stronger communities and a better quality of life for Indigenous Peoples. The Darlington New Nuclear Project shows what this can look like in practice. Through a $715 million federal-provincial loan guarantee, seven Williams Treaties First Nations are investing in the project and will collectively acquire a significant minority interest in the project, giving them a direct stake in a world-leading Canadian nuclear technology project and the long-term economic opportunities it will create. The Government of Canada has also begun discussions with eligible Indigenous groups in British Columbia and Alberta regarding the purchase of an ownership stake in the Trans Mountain Pipeline. The September 2026 offer to 128 Indigenous groups for a collective 15% ownership share in Trans Mountain Corporation marks an important milestone in fulfilling that commitment. The government also remains committed to pursuing a similar opportunity in relation to the Pacific Link project as it moves forward. Through these initiatives, along with ongoing and expanded support under the Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program , we are working in partnership with Indigenous leadership to help address historical barriers that have limited access to economic opportunities for Indigenous Peoples.

id: 2026|chap2-en.html|Giving Canadians a stake in what we build
chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Building a stronger, more sovereign economy
heading: Giving Canadians a stake in what we build
text: Through its plan to build Canada Strong, Canada's new government is prioritising nation-building projects that create jobs, attract investment, strengthen economic sovereignty, and position Canada for long-term growth. Canadians deserve a stake in this ambitious agenda. In the 2026 Spring Economic Update, we announced the Canada Strong Fund , Canada's first national sovereign wealth fund. This Fund is a powerful new tool for supporting our economic sovereignty while building long-term national wealth for Canadians. Once running, the Canada Strong Fund will invest alongside private sector investors in strategic, nation-building Canadian companies and projects. Canadians can also benefit directly from the Canada Strong Fund 's investments through the issuance of Canada Strong Notes , an investment product tied to the Fund's performance. These notes will enable Canadians to share in the Fund's returns, giving them a direct stake in the nation-building projects and companies in which the Fund invests. Where projects or companies have received federal support, the Canada Strong Fund will typically have co-investment opportunities on terms equivalent to those offered to private sector investors. The Fund will also have a mandate to selectively make strategic investments in high-potential projects and companies. The government will provide an initial $25 billion over three years to seed the Fund, which will grow over time through reinvested returns and other assets that may be allocated to it. Operating at arm's length and guided by a mandate to generate commercial returns, the Fund will help build a lasting pool of national wealth that supports Canada's long-term prosperity. Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to bring forward legislation in the coming months to establish the Canada Strong Fund as an arm's-length and standalone Crown corporation. In the interim period, the Canada Strong Fund will be incorporated as a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Canada Development Investment Corporation, with its own dedicated Board of Directors and Chief Executive Officer. Independence and professional management will ensure the Fund makes long-term, financially sound investment decisions in the best interests of Canadians. This governance structure strengthens transparency, credibility, and long-term performance. In 2027, the government intends to launch Canada Strong Notes , a retail investment product linked to the Canada Strong Fund that will give Canadians the opportunity to invest alongside the Fund and share directly in its returns . Designed to be broadly accessible, the Notes will be available to purchase through participating financial institutions. Canada Strong Notes will be easy to purchase, hold, and redeem. The Notes will provide principal protection, safeguarding Canadians' initial investment while allowing them to benefit from the Fund's performance. To execute its mandate, the Fund will develop a pipeline of investible opportunities through two main streams: Under Stream 1: Co-investments , the Fund will work closely with federal entities providing support to projects or companies (e.g., a loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank, a contribution agreement with the Strategic Response Fund ). Though the pathways may look slightly different for each individual circumstance, the provision of federal support – through another federal financing vehicle or the Major Projects Office – would normally include an opportunity to make a minority co-investment on terms that mirror those of private sector participants. Under Stream 2: Strategic Investments , the Fund will make selective investments on a commercial basis in high-potential projects and companies offering attractive long-term returns and supporting Canada's economic strength and resilience. A hydroelectric generation and transmission project referred to the Major Projects Office has received a recommendation to be included on the project list. As part of the Major Projects Office process, it works with the project proponent to secure an opportunity for the Canada Strong Fund to participate in financing this project. The Fund determines that this opportunity meets its risk-adjusted return targets, and it offers structured financing to the proponent (e.g., a long-term loan that has the option to convert to equity) along the same terms as its principal investor. This structure allows the Fund to help finance a major project through an investment that converts to equity once the project enters into service. The Canada Infrastructure Bank advances a concessional loan to enable road and power infrastructure to be built so a mining company developing a critical mineral project can reach a final investment decision. As part of the Bank's financial offering, it provides an opportunity for the Fund to make an equity investment based on terms set by the lead investor. A Canadian agricultural technology company has developed a platform to provide technology-driven farm solutions. The company has a proven track record of commercial success and is looking to position itself as a global leader. The Canada Strong Fund would conduct its own due diligence and provide a direct investment into the company alongside a lead investor on commercial terms, taking an equity position in a financing round priced by the market. The Fund's equity investment would help anchor and scale a Canadian company in a globally strategic and transformational technology. The government's recent commitment to make an equity investment in Cohere provides an example of the type of investment that could be undertaken by the Fund once established. The government has committed to invest in Cohere's Series E equity round on a commercial basis alongside private investors, taking a stake in a Canadian artificial intelligence company. This investment will help Cohere scale and compete globally, expand its computing infrastructure and Canadian workforce, and maintain its headquarters in Canada. Under a similar future scenario, the Fund would conduct its own due diligence and could invest alongside private sector investors on commercial terms, taking a minority equity position in a company. Such an investment could help anchor and scale a strategically important Canadian company while enabling Canadians to participate in the financial returns generated by its growth.

id: 2026|chap2-en.html|Managing Canada's trading relationship with the United States
chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Diversifying trade and deepening ties with reliable partners
heading: Managing Canada's trading relationship with the United States
text: For decades, Canada and the United States built one of the world's most integrated economic relationships, one that supported predictable access to each other's markets, major cross-border investment, and millions of jobs on both sides of the border. That relationship has fundamentally changed. We have recognised that the United States is altering all of its trade relationships, putting tariffs on its closest allies and charging for access to its vast market. Canada and the United States will not return to our old relationship. We have worked in that context to strike a fair deal that would provide the best access to the U.S. market and greater certainty to Canadian businesses and workers. Throughout, our goal has been to secure the best deal for Canadians, never a deal at any price or on any deadline. When the United States asked too much and offered too little, we chose to walk away rather than compromise Canada's sovereignty or put Canadian jobs at risk. In the face of these unjust tariffs, we are stepping in to protect and support our businesses and workers. We have provided nearly $44 billion in tariff relief support to industries and workers across Canada through a suite of programs including the Regional Tariff Response Initiative , the Strategic Response Fund , and support through the Business Development Bank of Canada . To protect Canadian interests and ensure our businesses compete on a level playing field, on September 8, 2026, Canada also announced proportional countermeasures on products targeted by the United States with rates matching U.S. tariffs. Other existing counter-tariffs against the United States, including on autos, remain in place. Canada's new government continues to believe that a mutually beneficial trade agreement is achievable. In seeking that path forward, our position is clear: any trade deal must respect Canada's sovereignty and the right of Canadians to determine our own economic future.

id: 2026|chap2-en.html|Opening new markets and strengthening reliable partnerships
chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Diversifying trade and deepening ties with reliable partners
heading: Opening new markets and strengthening reliable partnerships
text: Canada is a reliable global partner. We benefit from one of the most extensive networks of free trade agreements in the world, with preferential access to 1.5 billion consumers across 15 free trade agreements. This means Canada now has a market for our goods representing nearly two thirds of global GDP. But we recognise that long-term growth depends on reaching more customers in more markets. That is why we are working hard to further expand opportunities for Canadian exporters around the world. The government is on track to double Canada's market access and unlock preferential access to more than 3 billion consumers worldwide. To that end, it recently concluded trade agreements with Ecuador, Indonesia, and the United Arab Emirates, and is advancing efforts to complete new trade agreements in the coming months with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Philippines, India and Mercosur countries (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay). The government has also recently begun free trade negotiations with Thailand and Türkiye. Canada will also look to build on existing agreements, such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership and the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement. We are helping Canadian businesses take greater advantage of these agreements through trade missions, investment attraction efforts, and other initiatives to reach new customers. In recent months, Canada has launched negotiations on new tax treaties with Qatar and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and negotiations to update and modernise its tax treaty with Australia. These agreements will strengthen Canada's network of 93 tax treaties, reducing barriers to trade and investment with our key partners. Moving forward, the government will look to expand Canada's network of tax treaties to ensure that Canada remains a competitive location for future investments by pension funds and sovereign wealth funds. Canada and Europe are stronger together. As European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, "We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world." Deepening this partnership will help Canada and Europe secure greater strategic autonomy, build more resilient economies, and create substantial new opportunities for Canadians. The government has worked to strengthen Canada-EU relations and find opportunities for closer cooperation. Since Canada's new government was elected in spring 2025, Canada has become the first non-European participant in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), improving Canadian companies' access to joint defence procurement supported by the EU's €150 billion loan facility. We have also signed a Joint Declaration on Critical Minerals Collaboration to strengthen cooperation and multilateralism in support of more secure supply chains, bilateral investment and trade, and joint Canada-EU industrial competitiveness. These actions, alongside other agreements and negotiations, have laid the groundwork for this year's Canada-EU summit. At the Canada-EU summit in October 2026, the EU and Canada launched the Alliance for the Future — a new partnership of nations that will leverage the strategic capabilities of Canada, the EU, and a variable geometry of like-minded nations to address common issues, including strengthening our collective defence, giving us the deepest partnership possible short of accession. Additionally, Canada and the EU will work together in the coming months to make Canada the European Union's first Associate Member , and will discuss the scope and scale of this form of membership. At the Summit, Canada and the EU announced a series of measures to advance our strategic cooperation and deepen our partnership: Create new opportunities for Canadians More opportunities for Canadians to study, live, and work in Europe . Canada is launching negotiations to expand its participation in Erasmus+, Europe's flagship student and skills exchange program. Strengthen competition. Canada and the EU concluded negotiations on an updated Competition Cooperation Agreement, supporting fair competition, giving businesses a more level playing field, and helping protect consumers. Faster payment systems. Canada and the EU will support connecting Canada and the EU's instant payment systems to enable Canadians to send money to people and businesses in the EU seamlessly. More choice in banking and insurance. Canada and the EU will launch a Joint Working Group to explore opening their markets further to each other's banks, insurers, and fintech companies. Build more resilient economies Increase LNG exports. Canada and the EU will examine market conditions, infrastructure requirements, and other factors to assess the viability of increased exports. New ways to trade. Canada and the EU concluded negotiations on a landmark Digital Trade Agreement , reducing barriers, making our economic relations more resilient and future-ready, and reinforcing our cooperation. This agreement ensures that our trade relationship remains modern and reliable, and maintains strong safeguards for our peoples and their rights. Secure greater strategic autonomy Stronger critical minerals supply chains. Canada signed a new treaty framework with the European Investment Bank (EIB) to allow the EIB to invest in Canadian critical minerals projects that will provide the materials needed for defence and the energy transition. The government is also launching work to explore a raw materials stockpiling and investment framework to build more secure critical minerals supply chains. More options for navigation services . By partnering with the EU's Galileo program and the European Space Agency, Canada will strengthen positioning data and navigation services across Canada and the Arctic. Connect Canada and Europe through secure digital infrastructure. We are taking the first steps toward a new transatlantic data cable that would give Canada and Europe a direct, secure route for rapid data exchange—reducing reliance on a single provider. Increased production of Canadian-made waterbombers . Up to $2.5 billion in financing for Alberta-based De Havilland to dramatically increase waterbomber production capacity. This financing will help European partners and Canada fight wildfires and support thousands of jobs in Wheatland County, Alberta. Better connection for responding to disasters. Canada and the EU will explore cooperation on IRIS², one of the world's most advanced satellite systems. This satellite network will provide secure connectivity for governments, defence, and emergency services during crises. The new Alliance for the Future is built for people—Canadian and European. It helps students looking to study abroad, researchers collaborating to push the boundaries of what is possible, and entrepreneurs looking to reach new markets. Together, Canada and Europe are building a better, closer, more resilient future for our peoples, and we will continue to build ever-closer ties.

chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Diversifying trade and deepening ties with reliable partners
heading: Modernising trade systems
text: Canada's economy grows and competes when businesses can reliably get their goods and services to customers and when workers have access to good, high-paying jobs and opportunities. Recent consultations with industry, Indigenous partners, workers, and employers highlighted the importance of reliable supply chains, efficient trade corridors, and a modern labour relations framework: one that supports both economic resilience and workers' rights. To support investments in trade-enabling infrastructure and deliver on commitments made under the Trade Infrastructure Strategy announced in Budget 2025, the government launched the $5 billion Trade Diversification Corridors Fund and the $1 billion Arctic Infrastructure Fund . By reducing bottlenecks along key trade corridors, these investments will support more resilient supply chains, facilitate trade, and enhance competitiveness. As outlined in Section 2.1, Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act , will also strengthen trade corridors and transportation networks, help prevent disruptions to critical infrastructure, and support workers in federally regulated sectors. Modernising trade infrastructure extends beyond just building new ports, roads, and railways. It also means modernising the digital systems that vitally support trade and keep goods moving efficiently through supply chains. These systems allow businesses to exchange documents electronically, track shipments in real time, meet customs requirements, and arrange financing and insurance. Canada has made important progress in moving away from paper-based documentation, but we continue to lag many of our trading partners in using digital tools to move goods. To close this gap: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $55.3 million over two years on a cash basis, starting in 2026-27, to Transport Canada to advance digital trade processes. This funding would bring government and industry together to guide the work, update legislation and regulations, test new digital tools, and help businesses adopt them for a more competitive and productive trading environment. The threats posed by unfairly traded imports also risk harming our industries and workers. To protect Canadians, our trade remedy system allows duties to be imposed on unfairly priced or subsidised goods that are sold here in Canada. In 2025, these duties applied to approximately $3.3 billion in imports across industries employing more than 43,000 Canadians. As global trade patterns continue to shift, Canada needs a trade remedy system that can respond effectively to emerging unfair competition. To strengthen Canada's ability to respond to unfair trade: Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to launch public consultations on potential legislative and regulatory changes to strengthen this system and make it more efficient.

chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Diversifying trade and deepening ties with reliable partners
heading: Enhancing Canada's trade finance toolkit
text: In the face of shifting global trade and uncertainty, the government is helping Canadian businesses reach new markets and reduce their reliance on any single trading partner. We are deploying federal financing tools to help businesses expand internationally, unlock new opportunities, and overcome barriers to growth. One of these important tools is the Canada Account —a financing mechanism administered by Export Development Canada that supports high-impact projects and export transactions in our national interest. To ensure that the Canada Account continues to meet the needs of Canadian businesses: Budget 2026 proposes to introduce legislative amendments to increase the Canada Account limit and modernise its governance framework, providing greater flexibility to streamline approvals and support strategic, high-value transactions. Another tool is the Canadian Commercial Corporation (CCC) , which helps Canadian businesses sell their goods and services to international government buyers, creating more export opportunities across our economy. To better support Canadian exporters: Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to amend the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act, Export Development Act, and Financial Administration Act to make the CCC a subsidiary of Export Development Canada. This will better bring together two organisations dedicated to supporting Canadian exporters and allow for better alignment with federal priorities. These changes will ensure Canadian businesses have the financing and trade support they need to pursue opportunities abroad and grow in new markets.

chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Helping Canadians and their businesses navigate change
heading: Supporting Canadian workers and businesses
text: Historically, economic integration with great powers was a source of Canada's strength. More recently, it became a vulnerability, with tariffs being used as a tool of economic leverage. That is why we are building a stronger, more competitive Canadian economy at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad. We are reducing our reliance on one partner, and ensuring Canadian businesses can be more resilient in the face of global shocks. In Canada, we take care of each other. In times of crisis, we leave no one behind. That is why we are taking action to help Canadian workers and businesses withstand these pressures and emerge stronger. Workers affected by trade disruptions can access income and training supports to help them through difficult periods and prepare for new opportunities. Businesses of all sizes can get support to modernise their operations, improve their productivity, and access new markets. For companies that must import products from the United States, the government continues to provide a path to tariff relief through the United States Surtax Remission Order (2025) . Many businesses can qualify for relief automatically, without submitting an individual request. This includes: goods used by identified public health, public safety, and national security entities steel goods used in auto and aerospace manufacturing non-steel goods used in Canadian manufacturing, processing, food and beverage packaging, and agricultural production Relief is also available to any importer of more than 500 products that have been determined not to be produced in Canada . Companies not covered by this existing relief can apply to the Department of Finance Canada for individual remission. We continue to prioritise these requests and are dedicating additional resources to respond to heightened demand. $10 billion to help deliver reskilling and income support package for workers impacted by trade disruptions, including training and employment assistance, Workforce Alliances , and enhanced Employment Insurance supports. Enhanced Employment Insurance supports have benefited over 2.8 million workers and averted an estimated 30,000 layoffs. $12.9 billion to ensure access to liquidity and financing for businesses of all sizes through the Large Enterprise Tariff Loan Facility , the Business Development Bank of Canada's Pivot to Grow program, and temporary deferrals of corporate income tax and GST/HST remittances. This includes $1 billion in new lending made available by Farm Credit Canada. $20.6 billion to support firms affected by tariffs to pivot, grow, diversify markets, and maintain industrial capacity through the Strategic Response Fund , Regional Tariff Response Initiative , and other programming that provides targeted support to strategic sectors such as Forestry, Automotive, Metals, Mining, and Agriculture. Since the Spring Economic Update 2026, $16.6 billion of support has been announced for workers and businesses. In addition to targeted support for food security, forestry, and metals, this includes: An additional $6.1 billion to protect Ontario's steel industry, fortify its automotive industry, and build out Ontario's critical minerals supply chain, including in the Ring of Fire. An additional $1.5 billion through the Regional Tariff Response Initiative to provide cash and working capital to small- and medium-sized businesses, helping them maintain Canadian operations and retain employees in the face of tariffs. A new $500 million financing stream under the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC)'s Pivot to Grow program to help businesses manage immediate cash-flow pressures. Broader access to the BDC's tariff-related programs by lowering the minimum revenue requirement to $1 million, allowing more businesses to qualify for support. An additional $2 billion investment through the new Canada Strong Diversification Fund to help tariff-affected businesses move forward with shovel-ready projects, including those that will help repair, replace, or restore existing equipment and buildings. A new $3.5 billion package of Rapid Response Supports for Workers and Employers to help Canadians affected by tariffs. These include help to access income support through more flexible Employment Insurance rules and extended benefits for eligible workers, as well as improvements to JobBank.gc.ca, which helps workers find new opportunities. Employers can also access support through the new Workforce Retention and Retraining Program to help keep workers on the job and provide training during difficult periods. New flexibilities for the Large Enterprise Tariff Loan Facility , administered by the Canada Enterprise Emergency Funding Corporation, including increasing the amount of support available to firms and the maximum term of loans. Small- and medium-sized businesses are the backbone of Canada's economy. In every region and in every town of our country, they create jobs, support local economies, and make our communities good places to live. Today, faced with disruptive and unjustified tariffs, many small- and medium-sized businesses are fighting to protect jobs, maintain operations, and stay in business. The government has responded to these challenges by making its programs more accessible and responsive to the needs of small- and medium-sized businesses. This includes simplifying the application process for the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC)'s Pivot to Grow program, which has provided approximately $250 million in financing support through nearly 200 business loans to date, and lowering the minimum annual revenue requirement for BDC's direct tariff-related programs to $1 million so that more small businesses can access it. To help businesses cover payroll costs and defend Canadian jobs, industries, and supply chains, we have also enhanced the Regional Tariff Response Initiative (RTRI), delivered by Canada's regional development agencies. The RTRI provides two main forms of support. First, it supports investments that help businesses improve productivity and competitiveness, and reduce exposure to future trade disruptions, making them better equipped to succeed in a changing economy. Second, businesses can also use the RTRI to access liquidity assistance—financing to help maintain operations and keep workers on the job while they respond to trade disruptions and plan for the future. Since fall 2025, the RTRI has supported nearly $1.2 billion in investments for approximately 1,200 businesses, helping leverage an additional $2 billion from private and partner investments and supporting almost 25,000 jobs across Canada. Investments have been targeted to sectors most impacted by tariffs, including the steel and automotive industries. For example, regional development agencies have exceeded their targets for the steel and automotive sectors, investing more than $340 million in steel and almost $170 million in automotive, compared with targets of $150 million and $100 million, respectively. Building on this momentum, investments in the RTRI have reached nearly $3.5 billion. This includes additional support for sectors most affected by trade disruptions, including forestry, steel, copper, and aluminum, as well as sectors that help strengthen Canada's food security. id: 2026|chap2-en.html|Delivering more responsive regional support for businesses
chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Helping Canadians and their businesses navigate change
heading: Delivering more responsive regional support for businesses
text: Canada's regional development agencies are an important channel for supporting businesses and communities facing unique regional economic circumstances. They provide targeted support that protects jobs, strengthens local industries, and helps businesses respond to economic and trade-related disruptions. However, existing program parameters can limit the ability of regional development agencies to respond to the specific needs of businesses, including smaller firms. Greater flexibility would allow regional development programming to better respond to local economic conditions and emerging pressures. Budget 2026 announces that the government will be providing flexibility for regional development agencies to tailor support to smaller businesses and organisations across Canada, while maintaining appropriate fiscal oversight and accountability.

chapter: A more competitive and connected Canada
section: Helping Canadians and their businesses navigate change
heading: Supporting a more competitive wine sector
text: From grape growing and wine making to retail sales and tourism, Canada's wine sector supports Canadian careers and growing businesses in rural communities across Canada, from Niagara to the Okanagan Valley, and from the Eastern Townships to the Annapolis Valley. The sector is facing serious headwinds, including rising costs, labour shortages, tariffs, and severe weather events. Originally launched in July 2022, the Wine Sector Support Program provides financial support to licensed Canadian wineries to help them adapt to these challenges and remain competitive. To further strengthen Canada's wine sector: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $176.9 million over three years, starting in 2027-28, to Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada to renew the Wine Sector Support Program .
